speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: From a manpower perspective, there are several challenges for us, with the first being rising structural forces and unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What has been a worrying trend is that the layoffs especially affect professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) and the slower rate of re-entry into the workforce for this category of workers, especially those who are older in age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is largely due to what I have previously identified as the "three mismatches of skills, expectations and jobs".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, we face a long-term challenge to sustain inclusive quality growth, bearing in mind we have an ageing workforce, relatively flat productivity the past five years and a much slower employment growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With globalisation, Uberisation, digitisation, robotisation and the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the future jobs, workforce, skills, training, labour market and the future of work are rapidly evolving and transforming.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are several provisions which I believe can be further enhanced and improved in the EA and which the tripartite partners should examine to be relevant and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, an oddly drafted section 45 of the EA which sets out eligibility for retrenchment benefits, but it is phrased as a negative eligibility clause.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The section can be appropriately worded to give more certainty to the payment of retrenchment benefits and leaving the quantum to be negotiated, just as it is being done with collective bargaining.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The tripartite partners can also explore removing the two-year time bar, as shorter employment terms are more common now.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If removal is not possible, another possibility is to move this provision out of Part IV to the main body of the Act to be more inclusive since Part IV's application is limited.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest we further improve section 18A to provide more clarity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In particular, an inclusionary approach, such as a clearer and narrower definition of what situations are covered under section18A, would be a boon as the current provision is too broad and ambiguous.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The scope should be limited to a sale of business.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should clarify that outsourcing is not covered.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, transfers involving companies under receivership or judicial management should also be covered.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, a minimum notice period, of at least one month, should be stipulated and the notice should be in writing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To prevent multiple transfers, we should prohibit the transfer of the same group of employees for a period of one year after the first or subsequent transfers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Higher penalties specific to section 18A should be introduced and the union should be entitled to continue providing limited representation for up to two years so that PMEs do not lose protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the course of representing unions and union members in the Industrial Arbitration Court and advising unions on industrial relations issues, I have come across a number of situations in which the IRA does not envisage nor clearly address certain issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I will just confine them to two areas for now.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the status of Collective Agreement (CA) during a Judicial Management/ Receivership.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Other than having to formally apply for a leave of Court, there is limited scope for us to enforce a collective agreement or have recourse in the event of any non-compliance of the CA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I opine that the CA should continue to apply so as to protect the workers and there must also be an avenue for the union to enforce the CA during this moratorium in an economical yet expeditious manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Tripartite mediation is a very useful tripartite mechanism for alternative dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is also tightly linked to ECT as claims limits are raised if one goes via the tripartite mediation route.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although there is no salary cap, PMEs in certain categories where they are in management roles or where there may be conflict of interests as provided in the Act are excluded from utilising tripartite mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should also explore extending tripartite mediation to cover unfair dismissals of those outside the scope of EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am delighted that the ECT will come into operation next month.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The ECA currently covers all workers in an employment relationship but limited to 18 contractual and 43 statutory types of salary-related claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In light of an expected growth of freelance workers or what many call the "gig economy" in the next five to 10 years, the Labour Movement hopes more can become union members and enjoy the plethora of membership privileges the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and our unions offer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The above are my thoughts and suggestions based on the issues that confront us currently and which we need to address to ensure our labour laws are not just relevant but future-ready.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister for Manpower share the progress made with the manpower sectoral plans for the sectors that have already launched Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs)?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have the manpower sectoral plans been successful in helping companies in these sectors transform existing jobs as well as meet their manpower needs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore has a highly educated workforce, and professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) form more than 50% of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As business restructure, we need to pay special attention to this segment of workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Future of Jobs Report published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) in 2016 indicates that the greatest losses of jobs with the digital revolution will be in white-collar roles, with new jobs created in computer, technology and engineering related fields.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, Chinese characters always contain deep insights.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the character "企" which stands for "enterprise", it is made up of "人" or "people" on top, while the bottom part consists of "止" which means "cease", In other words, when there are people, there will be enterprises; if there are no people, then everything would come to a standstill.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, our workforce is saddled with two big challenges; the first being an ageing population, with the growth in the workforce shrinking every year; the second is the restructuring economy, bringing about changes to the labour force structure and skills.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The ageing population and low fertility rate has forced enterprises to leverage on technology to lessen the reliance on manual labour.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: While technology could improve productivity, workers need to be trained to use new technology.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For the older workers in particular, they need to make greater adjustments to attitude and mindset to cope with the demands of new skills.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Now, even the Government is encouraging civil servants to pick up digital technology.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is an outcome arising from the current environment.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some industries would gradually vanish, while some new industries would emerge.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The workforce needs to change its knowledge, skills and concept as quickly as possible in response to this transforming environment, and restructure, making the shift to new industries according to market needs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: It is impossible to solve the current manpower shortage in the short term.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As far as possible, we need to cater to society's needs, starting from basic education all the way to continuing education.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has already done much in the area of training.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Besides, the unemployed claim they cannot find jobs, while businesses perpetually say they cannot find workers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For many years now, the Workforce Development Agency and now SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG), has been working closely with the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry, helping many working people to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, we will continue to work with even more trade associations and industry associations to design training courses based on practical needs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As long as companies are supportive and employees who attend courses benefit from them, skills upgrading would form a trend, the quality of our entire workforce would be upgraded accordingly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Employers are taking longer to find suitable talent for the roles they have available and there is greater mismatch of skills to jobs created.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The good news is that there are good PMET jobs being created in Singapore and this trend is expected to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The bad news is that even though these jobs do exist, it does seem that PMETs impacted by restructuring and looking for jobs are not able to fill them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is MOM addressing the mismatch and missed matches, especially for PMETs and mature workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Which sectors will the new Attach and Train initiatives be focused on?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Apart from wage support for employers, what is the Government doing to ensure the quality of training and reskilling under the Adapt and Grow initiatives?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the Sectoral Manpower Plans for the six ITMs that are already launched, can the Minister share the success in matching the jobs created to the skills developed?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With technological advances, lower-skilled and repetitive jobs, both blue- and white-collar jobs are being replaced by automation, robots and artificial intelligence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For many low-skilled and low-wage workers, their jobs will go away.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What measures are in place to help these workers upskill to find good jobs and stay employed?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Last year, Minister Lim Swee Say had shared in Parliament that there are approximately 250 companies on the "triple-weak" watchlist.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Are the numbers of companies in this list going down or up?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For "triple-weak" companies that have been successful in getting off the watchlist, what have they done to strengthen the Singaporean Core in their workforce?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For flexibility and cost management, employment models are evolving with more companies hiring on contract terms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is MOM ensuring fair and progressive work practices for these workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is not necessarily bad as it allows freelancers with flexibility and scope to work beyond just what one company can offer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: However, freelancers do not get Central Provident Fund (CPF) nor make CPF contributions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This may impact their retirement planning and adequacy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In Singapore, CPF is core to planning for retirement adequacy and CPF funds allow for savings which could be used for healthcare and home ownership.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the changing employment landscape, are there any plans to have businesses make CPF contributions for the work they acquire from freelancers and for freelancers to make contributions to CPF beyond just to their MediSave?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Another area to pay attention to is the unequal impact that job disruptions will have on men and women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Data from the WEF Future of Work Report suggests that if current industry gender gap trends persist, and job transformation for new and emerging roles in computer, technology and engineering-related fields continue to outpace the rate at which women are currently entering these types of jobs, women are at risk of losing out on tomorrow's best job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With a highly-educated female population in Singapore and tight labour market, this is an area of both opportunity and focus.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Since the implementation of the Fair Consideration Framework, I wish to ask MOM how successful have we been in the drive towards hiring and developing a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In particular, can MOM share whether information and communications technology (ICT), financial sector and professional services continue to be among the top few industries where most of the watchlist companies are and whether we will impose even more punitive sanctions against those recalcitrant companies?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I also urge MOM to pay attention to employment agencies as, anecdotally, I hear from fellow PMETs that they are culprits of "hiring of their own kind" practices.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: One potential impediment is our National Service (NS) liability.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Next, we must also maintain a Singaporean Core leadership in every field and every industry if we want to see a truly vibrant Singapore with robust economic resilience in the face of challenges.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In respect of this, I am happy to see the introduction of the SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative in 2015 and the follow up by the Government in this year's Budget announcing that it intends to groom 800 potential leaders in the next three years.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I request the Minister to share more details on the initiative and how it intends to identify and groom these potential leaders.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is common knowledge that companies need high-quality staff to extend their businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many SMEs want to employ local talents, but some locals prefer to work for multinational corporations (MNCs), whether for prestige or better human resource (HR) benefits.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and trade associations and chambers (TACs) have to work closely together to meet market needs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, many locals stay away from construction-related work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, there are areas that pay well and need local talent.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, quantity surveyors (QSs) with three or more years of experience earn from $3,000 to $6,000.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But our polytechnics no longer conduct QS courses.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) conducts QS diploma courses with few local takers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One, can our Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) fill this gap?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Enhancing the skills and expertise of our local talent will allow us to rely on a larger and more stable workforce, compared to a foreign, transient workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two, can we also help with the marketing of SMEs by sectors, such as furniture, food and construction industries?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Help them with the brand imaging to make the industries more appealing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Poster boys and girls, inspirational stories, pride and mastery of skills, passion in doing a meaningful job − all these can help to build up the image of our important industries like construction and tourism.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: So long our workforce possesses the right type of skills, available in the right quantity, Singapore will remain an attractive place for investments, enterprise growth and entrepreneurship development.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In recent years, however, Singapore's indigenous workforce growth has slowed.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In addition, the Government has also reduced the inflow of foreign workers needed to augment our pool.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Coupled with rising worker levies and stricter dependency ratios, wages have risen.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: A number of economists have warned that "wage growth that outstrips labour productivity growth translates into declining profit margins, business closures and layoff of workers and, unless accompanied by a depreciation of the Singapore dollar, the increase in unit labour costs also implies a loss of international competitiveness." The latest international Institute for Management Development (IMD) report also says, "Singapore is losing its edge in drawing and keeping talent".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Worryingly, if this trend persists, Singapore will become less attractive for business and lose its ability to create good jobs.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: New investments may pass us by and existing businesses may relocate to more competitive economies.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would MOM help our workforce to remain internationally-competitive?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also helps SMEs to be more manpower-lean and helps them to improve their HR practices.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does MOM have a target number of SMEs to help and is the Ministry meeting the goal?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, would the Ministry share the profiles of companies under this scheme, for example, the sectors, types of businesses, sizes, number of employees and their nationalities?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During last year's COS debate, the Minister of State mentioned that the majority of applicants for the scheme were from the food and beverage (F&B) sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understandably, the F&B sector is labour-intensive and, therefore, is a prime candidate to benefit.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there more companies in labour-intensive sectors that have not come forward and would the Ministry consider more pro-active efforts in reaching out?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has there been any feedback on elements of the scheme that may not be compatible to different business models?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am also interested to know if MOM monitors the progress of the SMEs after they joined LEDS, with respect to their productivity levels, revenues and profit increases or gains in market share.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What types of changes in the companies' operations and transformations in work practices have resulted from LEDS?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More success stories can be shared to encourage others to take a closer look at how the scheme can help them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can the Minister share what progress have businesses made in Singapore, especially the SMEs, in terms of innovating to be less manpower-intensive, improving the quality of jobs and being more productive?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Have SMEs been able to restructure, create higher-skilled roles and transition from reliance on low-skilled foreign manpower to developing and recruiting locals?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Has the quality of jobs been enhanced and are there better jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: An emphasis of this year's Budget is the need to develop deep skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Key for businesses to becoming manpower-lean is to have manpower with deep skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What measures are in place to support and accelerate the building of deep capability, especially for SMEs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What measures are in place to continue to support businesses as they drive this transformation to become manpower-lean businesses?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are now at a crossroads, caught in the fastest changing business environment in decades while in a slower growth cycle.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: MOM's LEDS has been an innovative initiative to help companies at this crossroads.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government look into greater asset-pooling to reduce the capital expenditure (capex) needs of SMEs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry also share on the progress?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even though this is a slower period, it is also exactly the time to implement long overdue business changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that our SMEs will look into the following.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Management needs to also update their own skillsets, especially in digitalisation and technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Set time aside to train collectively as a company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, utilise Government funding to redesign business processes which is usually not possible when order books are filled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is robust growth in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) has outlined plans to support our global outreach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   I hope all of us can work in a determined and steadfast manner to achieve breakthrough in adversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important when jobseekers encounter job requirements that defer from what they had done in the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the extended use of wage support schemes that have overly broad coverage is a cause for concern, wage subsidies provided under the schemes of the Adapt and Grow initiative do not raise the same concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is because they are targeted at improving matching between employers and available workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Such schemes play an important role in helping both businesses and workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is neither possible nor desirable for businesses hit by economic weakness to completely rule out the option of shedding jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Adapt and Grow initiative helps workers to adapt to changing needs and grow in their capacity to handle higher-skilled jobs, thereby expanding their opportunities for regular employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This preserves the employment potential of workers who have been unemployed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the risk of participants not being offered permanent placements could be higher, the benefits of a rewarding career could also be higher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: First, would it be reasonable to expect that at least some of the participating employers must view it as being worth their while to hire under such arrangements even without Government wage subsidy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If that is so, what is the rationale for increasing wage support?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, how are schemes under the Adapt and Grow initiative evaluated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It should not just be assessed on their contributions to solving the short-term manpower shortages of participating companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By giving prospective hirings an early induction into the field, they could also enlarge the pool of eligible workers for such companies in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since such programmes address issues about matching, it should be useful to evaluate how the placements improve the capacity of participants to be matched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By helping employers understand the skills involved in their operations, they can also promote greater participation from employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I am thinking about this in terms of the skills frameworks under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: During the placement, will a worker placed under one of these schemes be expected to acquire certain key skills he/she did not have before, utilise those skills to add value to the participating employer?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, what does the placement process include?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some of these Singaporeans who face long-term unemployment, they are individuals with little formal education, low skills and little relevant experience who have difficulty looking for employment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them are seniors or above 50 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them are displaced because of disruptive technologies or are unwilling to accept jobs that pay lower salaries.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, some of them are in their 20s or 30s and are tertiary-educated but still are not able to gain longer-term employment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met residents who are either university or polytechnic graduates but who have difficulty finding employment after leaving or being retrenched from their first job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of them graduated with a first degree in Engineering.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, when the company he was working with closed down because of poor business, he found himself unemployed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a young son just born, he tried applying for another job as an engineer.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Six months into his job search, he was still not able to secure an engineering job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the end, he took up a part-time position doing administrative work just so he can earn an income to support his young family.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or could it be due to a mismatch of expectations between them and prospective employers with regard to salaries, work responsibilities or work hours?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: About 70% of them are PMEs aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some take six to nine months while others take longer to find suitable employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Older PMEs have it tougher in terms of re-entry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Those in their 30s are also not spared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have three points to put forward to MOM.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I call it the "3Ms" of Mentoring and Case Management, Mid-Career Entry and Mindsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: First, helping the long-term unemployed requires a case management approach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We need to adopt a one-to-one or one-to-few approach and not a one-to-many approach, unlike traditional job placements and career fairs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These long-term unemployed require more than just counselling or being notified of career fairs or job openings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, one particular observation I have with the PCP is that when PMEs move into a new sector or totally new job, he/she enters at the entry point of that new sector or job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I find this unsatisfactory considering mature PMEs have accumulated decades of work experience and skill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, mindsets have to change, not just employees but employers as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Ability is vital because we need skills for current and future jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Agility is not just about being able to change but change quickly and flexibly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Adaptability is crucial with shorter economic cycles, job obsolescence, new forms of work and new work streams.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We need a new work mindset to embrace change before change embraces us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must not forget the younger PMEs, who have their own unique problems as a sizeable segment in the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, young PMEs are now also facing substantial risks of being laid off and affected by restructuring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another issue is that many young PMEs have been switching to contracts for service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many are doing it for the flexibility of time and space, while some are doing it to expand the market for their skills, so that they can be engaged by overseas companies paying a better price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this also makes them more vulnerable to abuse and exploitation, especially since they will not be able to lodge claims and obtain assistance through the usual channels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The last issue I would like to highlight is that in this category of young PMEs are many young mothers who would like to return to work after a period of leaving the workforce to care for infants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was a well-attended career fair organised by social enterprises last year that for the first time catered to women returning to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope Workforce Singapore could look into career services targeting this special group of young PMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We have not eradicated ageism and the rapid pace of technological changes make getting new jobs and career transition difficult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Adapt and Grow is an important policy to help these workers adapt to a new work and economic environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Second, PCP can be enhanced by lowering the entry requirements and the duration of training.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It can be intermediate job grades and functions before the full conversion is done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Third, Attach and Train can be a gamechanger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The entry salary should use PCP's as a benchmark.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I also encourage the public sector to participate actively in Attach and Train.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This unit can look at evolving the Jobs Bank for age-friendly employers, develop employability programmes and train specialised coaches to help them navigate the job market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: In addition, we can also create new jobs in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The Northeast Community Development Council's (CDC's) Community Employment Programme developed by Mayor Teo Ser Luck is a good example of how seniors can be productively hired for community work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: To evolve the programme further, we should work with companies, such as Honestbee, to create micro jobs accessible to our more senior residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Supporting our middle-age and older workers is not only the Government's responsibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: In an ageing Singapore, they can be the vibrant driver of growth if we give them opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: They have carried Singapore's development on their backs over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is time and imperative that Singapore give these veteran soldiers their second wind.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Or that those who face unemployment are individuals with little formal education, low skills or little work experience.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, increasingly, this is no longer the case.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: A resident I know, Daniel, has a degree in computer science from one of our local autonomous universities (AUs), which he obtained about 20 years ago.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: He held a stable and well-paying job in an MNC dealing with computers and information technology (IT) for about 15 years before he was retrenched from the position due to internal restructuring and the dissolution of the department he was in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: In other words, he found himself facing job redundancy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Since then, he has been looking for employment and only managed to get short-term contract work, now and then, if he is lucky.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Daniel is tertiary-educated, has about 15 years of work experience in the IT sector and is now in his early 40s.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Yet, he has difficulty getting a job even though his expectation for a monthly salary is lower than that for a new university graduate.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I feel extremely sorry for him and have also tried to personally help him gain employment to no avail, as yet.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Another resident, Saiful, a polytechnic graduate in the marine and offshore sector, worked for three years in the industry.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: He left his job to look for a better paying one but after months of futile job-searching, resorted to working as a security guard.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: He has worked as a security guard for the past two years as he could not find a job in the marine and offshore sector.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: He is in his late 20s and is already facing employment difficulty.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: With the current state of the economy and employment market, I am sure there are many more in the same predicament as these residents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What is its impact for this group of employees?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Under PCP, how do we ensure that those who undergo PCP will not always start at the bottom of the rung in the new industry in which they have joined because they do not have the relevant experience or simply because they are quite desperate to just find employment?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does MOM keep track of how long they remain in their new jobs and their subsequent progress, and can the Minister share these statistics?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: He also mentioned there are mismatches between the number of applicants and number of job openings across these 50 PCPs and that MOM is trying to minimise the imbalance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Can the Minister share more details on how this is being resolved?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) has identified Healthcare, IT, Telecommunications and Aviation as our growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Thousands of jobs in civil, computer and precision engineering, project management, software development, systems analysis and design, data science and robotics will be created.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Will MOM be looking into PCPs for such positions?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: So far, the PCP is reactive in nature.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Most applicants would have lost their jobs before they enrol.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: MOM may consider publicising PCPs to feed the needs of growth sectors and co-design modular training courses with the participating employers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is so that interested applicants, who may still be employed but at risk of redundancy, can join in the training in the evenings and weekends, similar to pursuing an additional degree or certification.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This would offer a smoother transition for the affected PMETs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The Attach and Train initiative was announced by the Finance Minister for sectors that have good growth prospects but where companies are not ready to hire.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry elaborate on what these sectors are, the types of companies within these sectors that would be eligible for this programme and the eligibility criteria?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have a support system and support group to engage the affected PMETs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I have received feedback from affected PMETs that they have to start at a low level in terms of salary and grade in their new profession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: While the PMETs mentioned that they are appreciative of the effort of the Government, they feel that it can be quite painful for them and their family having to see them, especially the main breadwinner, to start at a low level and having to live with a reduced salary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I urge them to be patient and encourage them to do well in their new career while my Parliamentary colleagues and I engage the Government to improve the PCP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: During his Budget speech, I am very pleased that Minister Heng mentioned that there will be enhancements to the Adapt and Grow initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what enhancements will be made to PCP?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Can MOM share an update with the latest statistics on the progress of CSP, such as the number of PMETs in the various job functions and sectors under CSP and the sectors which have been conducive for CSP?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: SMEs can seek help from Workforce Singapore (WSG) to recruit PMETs through CSP.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: With more SMEs encouraged to expand overseas, it will be a win-win situation if experienced PMETs with an MNC background with overseas exposure can be matched with such SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Will MOM consider enhancing CSP by actively facilitating such matches?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: For this subset of CSP employees, can the period of support be extended beyond a year as projects involving foreign markets may have long gestation periods?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does MOM follow up with CSP placements and monitor their progress?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: And were there cases where the CSP placements did not work out as envisaged?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These insights will help to refine the programme such that it is beneficial to both the PMETs placed and the SMEs hiring them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: If the benefits are viewed as being one-sided, then the good intentions of the programme would be lost.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have two recommendations to enhance the effectiveness of the Jobs Bank in facilitating job-matching.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, a key challenge in job-matching is ensuring that there is a match between an employee's skill and the job requirements as well as between expectation of employers and employees regarding the job.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Jobs Bank can enhance skills matching by allowing jobseekers who have just completed training courses to be automatically directed to job openings that require those skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This dynamic matching does not only facilitate the job hunting process, but it will also help jobseekers recognise the value of learning new skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, I would like to propose that non-Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) training providers be subject to a certification standard TrainTrust which can be modelled on EduTrust.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To encourage providers to come on board, courses and providers that are TrainTrust-certified can be given priority on the list of courses that are recommended to Jobs Bank users.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A certification standard will go some way in ensuring the quality of skills learnt has strengthened the trust of the potential employers in the courses attended or certification obtained by the jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It will provide a reassurance to jobseekers on the values of the certification that they are spending time and effort to earn.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I also have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I feel that the Jobs Bank has an important role to play in minimising the mismatches and missed matches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Moving forward, I have five new suggestions for MOM and WSG to consider.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: First, applications through the Jobs Bank are without acknowledgement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some question whether employers are just paying lip service by posting job advertisements merely to fulfil the mandatory requirement for EP applications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Is there a way we can make the employing company at least acknowledge the receipt of the job application and update whether the vacancy has been filled or that the applicant is unsuccessful?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As highlighted previously, there should be some way to confirm or audit the Jobs Bank to confirm the veracity and validity of the job openings as some businesses may post non-existent job ads to boost up investor relations and confidence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: For higher paid jobseekers, they will go to the executive search firms and headhunters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Maybe an awareness campaign can be run to improve the public's perception of the Jobs Bank and promote the universal adoption of the Jobs Bank by all employers and businesses so that all will use it to post all their job vacancies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, beyond job advertisements and to help narrow the skills gap, the Jobs Bank can be enhanced with a skills gap analysis feature by comparing the applicants' curriculum vitae (CV) with the desired job's requirement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fourth, a comprehensive big data analytics module can also be incorporated into the Jobs Bank to educate jobseekers with the trends and types of in-demand skills that employers desire.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am aware it is not mentioned in the current Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is crucial to the current tight labour market against the backdrop of global uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we are to encourage more groups of people to remain contributing members of the labour force − mothers, women returning to the workforce after a hiatus, the elderly and those with handicaps – their rights must be protected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also ensure that in our multiracial and cosmopolitan city, all workers, regardless of gender, race, religion, disabilities and also recently those in the "gig economy", have access to an accommodating and empathetic job market that respects their right to contribute and grow as any regular employee.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Indirectly, workers have also gained through better jobs and wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: They are also motivated to find even better ways to implement the projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I believe there is scope to expand such an approach to other Government schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I note that not all gains are realised quickly and might neither be shared readily nor easily quantifiable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I propose that we expand gains-sharing to include investment in workers' training, such as subsidising training courses or providing training leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: In such a way, there will be longer-term entrenched benefits for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Government also consider making this expanded definition of gains-sharing a key performance indicator (KPI) for our grants and initiatives?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I shared with the House that there were companies which had the locals' interests in their hearts, although they had a regular EP inflow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Can the Minister share the profile of these firms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: How have these efforts encouraged these firms to employ more Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: How have other firms responded to this signal?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is unlike the traditional Place and Train scheme where workers are trained after they have been hired for jobs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This way, workers can still stand a chance to be trained on the job and gain experience while trying out new sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I wish to further call upon the Ministry to do more for "mumpreneurs" who would appreciate flexible work arrangements (FWAs), such as working from home.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Government can consider providing grants or tax reductions for costs in setting up and running of home offices for this group of women entrepreneurs?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I wish to speak on re-entry and re-employment of women and having enough in their nest egg for their old age.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the CPF Board's report in 2013, there seems to be a significant improvement in women's CPF balances.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, this analysis was done with women aged 25-54.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For the elderly aged 55 and above, they may lack savings and rely greatly on contributions by family members and assistance from the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can informal jobs, such as caregiving within the family and friends, be incentivised in terms of Government MediSave top-ups?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The tripartite approach to address age management and employment concerns is, indeed, commendable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, as women live longer, it would be worthy to drill further down the concerns of mature women and their needs as they age beyond 60, whether or not they are in employment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Another area of frustration of many Singaporeans is that they work in a company where the majority of employees are foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can MOM update this House on the actions taken by the Government to reduce such unfair and unethical practices and what measures are there to protect Singaporean workers?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We need to assure Singaporean employees that the Government does not condone such behaviour of employers who discriminate against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Are there any punitive actions taken against any such companies found to have flouted MOM's regulations?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is also important for MOM to signal to employers that there are severe consequences if they take advantage of policies to employ mainly foreigners in their companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In such a case, we might as well not allow such companies to operate in Singapore as there is no benefit to the country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For recalcitrant companies, would MOM consider cancelling the Work Permits or EPs of these companies?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a drastic action but I cannot see the benefit of having such companies operate in Singapore if they do not provide sufficient employment for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, during the Budget Debate, I appealed to MOM to consider a mandatory retrenchment benefit law for workers who had lost their jobs due to retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: MOM had then shared about their schemes to help workers who were retrenched.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I was particularly impressed by the Adapt and Grow initiative and CSP which provided wage support for companies which employ eligible Singaporean PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, the Government is helping companies with their wage bill if they employ retrenched workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There have also been tripartite guidelines given requiring employers to inform MOM within five days of laying off workers and to provide the employees' details.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Unfortunately, as can be seen from a recent case when an employer terminated several workers on grounds of poor performance, employees who lose their jobs for whatever reasons will face a certain period of financial uncertainty in their lives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If retrenchment benefits are made compulsory, only a small number of workers will be affected.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But making retrenchment benefits compulsory would certainly help these workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And to the worker who is retrenched without any compensation, it is really a frustrating time for him as he struggles to provide for his family.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: NTUC Deputy Secretary-General Heng Chee How and several Members had shared that, on the ground, there is growing concern on job opportunities and job security.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we transform to take our Singapore economy into the future, some may wonder what the future economy will bring us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Will the rise of the digital and gig economy change the employment landscape, resulting in less employment and more freelancing?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In short, will we have enough jobs, enough good jobs, or will more workers be hit by unemployment, under-employment and structural unemployment?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The purpose of us transforming towards our future economy is to improve our jobs, our careers, our lives, not to make them worse.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, there is no guarantee that all economic transformations will be successful, as seen in failures in some countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But for Singapore, we have succeeded time and time again, so far.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, working together, whole-of-Singapore, we must make sure that we succeed again.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will not be easy because to open the door to a future of good jobs and better careers for all our people, we must have not one, not two, but actually four keys in our hand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The first key is the key of Quality Job Creation, to create enough jobs of good enough quality for everyone, young and old, PMETs and rank-and-file.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Externally, due to business uncertainty, companies are hiring less.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But, more importantly, internally, our local workforce growth has slowed quite significantly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With ageing and low birth rate, coupled with an already high labour force participation rate, local workforce growth is heading for stagnation over the next 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It will pick up again when business sentiment improves.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But slowdown in our local workforce growth is structural.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Hence, if we try to bring employment growth back to 100,000 a year, we will need to bring in many more foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we take in 50,000 more a year, this will mean 500,000 over 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Higher economic gains will come with even higher social costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have little choice but to learn how to grow our economy with a workforce growth of about 1% from now on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This means about 33,000 net increase in total employment a year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There will be fluctuations from year to year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some years less, maybe 25,000; some years more, maybe 40,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, 25,000 to 40,000, this range should be achievable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But even so, we will still be faced with the challenge of rising under-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will happen when the improvement in job quality − not just new jobs, but also existing jobs − is not able to keep pace with improvement in the education and skills profile of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So far, the overall quality of our local employment has been improving.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we help every worker to upgrade to become a better worker, we need to make every job a better job, every career a better career.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I believe we can, but only if we look at technology not as our competitor for jobs, but as our partner in the creation of jobs, quality jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We can either use it to our advantage or allow our competitors to use it to our disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To be on the winning side, we need to keep crossing the technology gate, better and faster than the competition, so that we will not end up in the black hole of global competition.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, with so many innovations out there, crossing the first gate of technology is essential but will not be enough.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There is still the second gate to cross − the market gate − to compete successfully for customers and build market share.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those who fail again will end up in the black hole of global competition.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To cross the two gates, we have been building our bridge of innovation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our next challenge is to make this bridge of innovation longer, stronger and wider, so that many more can get through as individual companies, as clusters of industry and as one future economy; not just the Pioneers, not just the early adopters, but the early majority and, eventually, the late majority as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some may wonder, the more we strengthen the bridge of innovation, would technology not take away even more jobs from us?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Craftmark is a distributor and retailer of over 20 brands of footwear and leather goods and accessories.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the use of radio-frequency identification (RFID), it cuts down manhours for stocktaking by 90%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, they achieved not just better business for the owners but also better jobs for the workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the key words for MOM are "Better Jobs".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Soup Spoon is a popular restaurant chain with more than 20 outlets.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To expand overseas, the company decided to move from food retail to include food manufacturing as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With automated packaging process, its operation is not only competitive, but also 25% more manpower-lean.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the key words for MOM are "Manpower-lean".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Tiong Seng is a market leader in construction.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To maximise the impact of using a technology known as BIM, the company helps all its subcontractors to adopt the same technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the key words for MOM are "Productivity Gain".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Instead of worrying about technology taking away our jobs, we should focus more on how to partner technology to take away customers and jobs from our competitors before they do it to us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is why over a year ago, MOM initiated LEDS to bring various agencies together, to provide a one-stop service, making it easier for the SMEs to develop business capability, manpower and markets.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Where necessary, MOM is even prepared to allow short-term flexibility on foreign manpower quota to help make changes happen faster.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Ms Jessica Tan asked about the progress.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Among them were the three I cited earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This year, we will go three steps further.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, we will strengthen the scope of LEDS with new schemes introduced this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our agency partners will help more SMEs to go digital as well as to expand market overseas.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Second, we will speed up the development and deployment of what we call "Cluster" solutions and promote their widespread adoption, not just by the individual companies but by clusters of companies, in a cheaper, better and faster way.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Thirdly, we will work closely with sectors that are facing and will continue to face manpower shortages due to ageing of their existing workforce or growing demand for labour.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will support BCA and the industry to upgrade existing workers and attract and train more locals to strengthen our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: My colleague Minister of State Teo Ser Luck will speak more on the key thrusts of our Transform and Grow efforts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we will still face the risk of the third kind, which is structural unemployment, a result of mismatches in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We, therefore, need a second key − the key of Workforce Adaptability.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must help our people to adapt to change, take on better jobs − both new and existing jobs − and build new careers we are creating for them in our future economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The profile of jobseekers we assisted is inclusive – young and old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh may be pleased to note that about 45% were in their 20s and 30s.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Likewise, we helped workers who are employed, unemployed and long-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Among the unemployed, 40% of them who found jobs last year, were long-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Also, the split between PMETs and rank-and-file is about 50-50.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But a majority of jobseekers are what we call the missed match cases.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is just that they have yet to find each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we help them to plan their careers, search for jobs, prepare their CVs for interviews, and more than 16,000 workers ─ what we call the missed match workers ─ found jobs successfully.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To help more jobseekers and employers to find each other, we will make better use of technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have improved the user friendliness of the National Jobs Bank to provide better search functions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I recall there was feedback given by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Jobseekers are also better updated on their application status, a point raised by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we have not mandated both the employers and jobseekers to inform us of successful job placements, I do not have the statistics that Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap asked for.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, the National Jobs Bank is a place for employers and workers to find each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: WSG and MOM are not in the loop, but we provide the platform for them to find each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have also piloted Virtual Career Fairs which are of a longer duration than the physical job fairs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It will enable various groups of jobseekers to search for what types of jobs they are looking for.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, First Jobs for young graduates, Next Jobs for those in mid-career, and Next Careers for those changing profession.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We also linked up the online marketplace with the Individual Learning Portfolio portal to be launched by SSG so that we can provide seamless access between the two ─ from skills to jobs, from jobs to skills, as suggested by Mr Patrick Tay as well as Mr Desmond Choo during the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These major enhancements will be rolled out progressively this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will keep enhancing the online marketplace facilities, including the useful suggestions by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Besides using technology to widen our outreach to more jobs and more jobseekers, we will also expand the channels of job-matching services through closer collaboration with private sector employment agencies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having explored with leading employment agencies, both locally and overseas, we are now ready to partner two leading employment agencies which have been working with the government agencies in the UK and Australia.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though the current split between missed matches and mismatches is about 75:25, we expect to see a continued shift towards more mismatches in the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Structural unemployment is sticky and harder to solve.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, it is better that we act faster and act more proactively.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, at the COS, we introduced the Adapt and Grow initiative to help PMETs who need the extra help in overcoming these missed matches.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This year, we are enhancing the Adapt and Grow initiative again.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we support businesses to transform and grow faster, more old jobs will be destroyed, more new jobs will be created, and more existing jobs will be recreated.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the past, we strived for lifelong employment for our workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, with keener and stronger competition, instead of lifelong employment, one career, one employer for life, we now have lifelong career.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One career but with many different employers throughout our working life.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the future, lifelong career will go, too, giving way to what I call lifelong re-employability, meaning not just many employers, but also many careers in our lifetime.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Each time, when we move from one career to another career, we will have to learn new skills, adapt to new environment, to regain our employability time and time again.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we can expect to see more PMET jobseekers facing three growing mismatches in future: job mismatch, skill mismatch and wage mismatch.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, we launched 36 new PCPs to help more than 1,000 PMETs to switch careers and to take on job openings in those sectors that are still growing and hiring.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One of the new PCPs is for data analytics.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One company, as they moved on into smart manufacturing, they created new roles, such as data analytics.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But at the same time, some of the existing jobs and staff were at risk of being let go.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Instead of retrenchment, WSG, the company and a training provider, worked together to retrain these redundant workers who are mostly more than 40 years old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Building on their domain expertise, they are now leading projects using their new skills in data analytics.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, with professional conversion, these PMETs have moved into an emerging area with potential for career growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, they can look forward to becoming data scientists and programme managers one day.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is a point that several Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong may be pleased to know that the PCP participants, not all of them, wait till they are unemployed before they join PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, about half, or maybe even more than half of them, are still in employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I believe they are what the Secretary-General of the NTUC called "the future retrenched".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These PCP participants, they are actually in employment today, but still they have decided to take up PCP to convert into their new professions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because when they look at where they are today, either they feel that they could be at risk of being retrenched in the future, made redundant in the future, or maybe the new career can offer them better growth prospects.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, I want to assure this House that for PCP, we are targeting at both the redundant workers of today, as well as the redundant workers of tomorrow, to help them take on careers of the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These are the concerns raised by Mr Patrick Tay, Dr Intan Mokhtar, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What this means is that, under PCP, since we support 70% of the wages, at $4,000, we will be able to support PCP jobs with a salary of up to $5,700.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Together, we can fund mid-level jobs of up to $5,700.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, at $6,000, we will be able to support PCP jobs of a salary of up to $6,700.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With these enhancements, for a PCP of six months conversion period, we are able to support up to $24,000 worth of salary.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For mature PMETs or those who are long-term unemployed, salary support can be up to $36,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is on top of the training subsidies of an average of $9,000 for a six-month PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To equip PMETs with the new skills needed for the future and ensure that they are able to put the new skills to good use, we have all along been adopting Place and Train, that is, place first and train later approach for PCP, and this has worked well up to now.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we now face a new bottleneck because during this period of economic transition, the pace of hiring is slower, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though there is a demand for manpower to meet future needs but, in some sectors, companies are holding back hiring due to business uncertainty in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This poses a problem for both the jobseekers and the employers because training for conversion takes time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, precious time is wasted if we have to wait until the employers are ready to hire before we start skills conversion, a point echoed by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To overcome this, we will introduce Attach and Train to convert PMETs ahead of job placement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I just want to clarify one point made by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan, which is that Attach and Train is not targeted at companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Attach and Train is targeted at industries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we do not choose companies to support, but we choose industries to train these PMETs ahead of job placement for the industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Since there is no employer, so we do not pay wage support to the employers but, instead, we pay these training allowances to the PCP trainees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To lower the risk of non-placement, trainees are attached to companies as an integral part of the conversion process.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, they do not just attend classroom training.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, they have to be attached to companies, equivalent to working in a real-life environment, to learn the conversion in a real-life environment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to familiarise them with their new jobs and new workplace, so that they will be more job-ready when companies are ready to hire them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To minimise potential abuse by employers, we will select a few sectors to start with and manage the programmes closely with our industry partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, it is not a programme for all sectors but only for selected sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: How do we go about selecting these sectors?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The criteria are the outlook for sector growth must be promising; industry leaders must be committed to help select and place trainees and rally the support of the industry members; they must also be committed to jointly spearhead industry transformation and manpower development for their respective sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, the sector has in place a professional conversion facility known as SCALA, and the interest from PMETs is high.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, when SCALA conducted their first PCP course, they had 80 training places, but they received 250 applications.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But at that time, there were only 43 jobs from 14 companies and, as a result, 37 of the PCP places were wasted.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the introduction of Attach and Train, we will be able to take in more PMETs for future courses, train them, attach them to potential employers, help them to be more job-ready when companies are ready to hire them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked about the progress of various Sectoral Manpower Plans (SMPs) and support for the respective ITMs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More will be done as and when more ITMs are launched.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about support for the SMEs and the various sectors, such as construction.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Other potential industries for the Attach and Train include infocomm.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are looking at IT system administrator − apparently there is a shortage of them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also looking at healthcare, in consultation with the Ministry of Health (MOH), and also biologics, which is a new growth sector in manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also partner NTUC to help more workers to migrate into future growth sectors, something that the Secretary-General of NTUC is most passionate about.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To encourage employers to hire mid-career PMETs, we provide wage support through CSP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked why the need to subsidise wages.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: By reducing wage cut for the affected PMETs and reducing wage costs for the employers, during this transitional period for up to one year, we hope to bring more of them together for both sides to know each other better, so that they can continue employment without our wage support after the transitional period.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Sim Lay Koon was previously a finance manager.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She left her job in mid-2015 due to job misfit.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The job search took longer than expected, so she took the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA) certification while looking for a job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the help of CSP, her new employer was prepared to give her a chance and to try her out in a role which is slightly bigger and different from what she used to do in her previous job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She is now a senior accounts associate doing accounting for the SME clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Sim used to be doing accounts for her own company but now, in her new job, she is doing accounts for the SME clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is something different but, with the support of CSP, both sides were prepared to have a go and, so far, things have worked out well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, the new employer is so supportive of her that her employer would grant her a half-day time-off every week for her to complete her final ACCA module.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked for the progress of CSP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To help more PMETs affected by redundancy, especially those who are long-term unemployed (LTU), a point raised by Dr Intan Mokhtar and Mr Patrick Tay, this year, we will enhance our support for three groups of PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, the mature PMETs who are unemployed and have been actively looking for jobs for more than one year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are not just LTU; they are longer-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Currently, those aged 40-49 receive a lower level of support compared to those who are aged 50 and above.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have decided to combine the two groups.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Now, those aged 40-49 will receive the same level of support as those who are more than 50 years old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What this means is that we will double our wage support for this group aged 40-49.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In total, we support up to $25,200 of wage support over one year for the employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, younger PMETs who are in their 20s or 30s can now receive 20% of wage support for the first six months; 10% of wage support for the second six months; a total wage support of up to $12,600, even if they have not been made redundant.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As long as they are LTU, they will qualify for CSP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also enhance CSP to help match more PMETs to SMEs, a concern expressed by Miss Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The qualifying salary for CSP is currently set at $4,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I want to emphasise that this is not to depress wages for the PMETs but to increase job opportunities, especially for the younger PMETs who are LTU.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also allow the hiring of PMETs for overseas job assignments, as long as the employees meet the criteria of CSP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For those having greater difficulty finding jobs, we believe it is useful for them to try out the jobs and employers before taking up the jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
