text: Likewise, employers want to try out the jobseekers, too, before they are ready to make the offer for employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: SDB Solutions is a company that specialises in digitising and archiving hardcopy documents.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The work requires patience, precision and attention to details, and they find it challenging to find workers of the right fit.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under the Work Trial programme, they tried out five jobseekers for two weeks, and three of them decided to continue with the job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She stopped work for 11 years to raise her children and she was not sure whether she can do the job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After the two weeks of work trial, it turned out to be a good fit.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, the company, SDB Solutions, is so happy that it is now offering three more Work Trial places under the programme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: During or at the end of the work trial, if the employers offer employment to these rank-and-file workers who have been unemployed for more than one year, we will provide wage support of 30%, capped at $600, for the first six months of employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, those who are LTU workers for one year or more, we put them on a work trial, we support them up to three months, and during or at the end of the attachment, if the employer offers him or her the employment, we will subsidise the wages of 30%, up to $600 for the first six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The whole purpose is to help as many of our LTU workers to go back to work and, hopefully, stay on the job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These workers will also get an additional incentive payment of $1,000 for staying in the job for at least six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To support inclusiveness at our workplaces, this enhanced Work Trial also supports Persons-with-Disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will partner NTUC to tap on the various support schemes under Adapt and Grow to support this Returnship Programme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Members shared during the Budget Debate some unhappy cases where jobseekers did not succeed in finding jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the rank-and-file workers, our success rate currently is about 70%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One of our unsuccessful rank-and-file cases is Mr A.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He left his job as a logistics assistant due to differences with his boss.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He had specific expectations in his job search − it must be within four bus stops from where he lives; work only from 9.00 am to 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He demanded that the career coach must arrange at least two job interviews every week for him until he found a suitable job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And he refused our help to improve his resume and interview skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With his unrealistic expectations, uncooperative and demanding attitude, we have not been able to help him to secure any job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have not given up on him, even though he has been uncontactable for six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In contrast, Ms B, 50 years old, is a successful rank-and-file case.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She is a single-income parent supporting two children and an elderly mother.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She has a brain tumour, but under control.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She left her previous job as a property consultant and approached our career centre after 10 months of unsuccessful job search.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She needs to work near her home and end work at 5.00 pm every day due to family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She told her career coach what she wanted.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It must be senior management position in investment banking, minimum pay of $10,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But she was unreceptive to advice to enhance her resume and improve on her interview skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When rejected by potential employers, she demanded that the employers must share with her the resumes of the successful candidates to verify that they were actually more qualified than her.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She even verbally abused our staff on several occasions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the current status of such a case, it is "no successful outcome".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On a positive note, Mr D, 47, is a successful PMET case.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He worked for more than 20 years as a plant manager.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He spent the last 10 years based in China.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He lost his job when the factory closed down.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And the last time he looked for a job, it was more than 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He did not know how best to search for jobs, so he sent out his resume blindly to 70 companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After eight months, he approached WSG career centre.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our career coach helped him discover his strengths and teach him how to market his strengths to the potential employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We helped him to improve his resume to better reflect his capabilities and experience.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He attended career fairs and walk-in interviews whenever there were opportunities.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the support of CSP, he secured a job as a production manager without having to suffer any wage cut.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is the result of good teamwork between the jobseeker and career coach.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Likewise, when the outcomes are negative, please do not put all the blame on our career coaches.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Please remember this is a joint responsibility, and we can only help those who want to help themselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Every time I talk to our career coaches at WSG and e2i − we have about 120 of them − I am struck by their competence, passion and dedication.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are certified career development facilitators, with skills in group facilitation, basic counselling, emotional support, use of psychometric and career-matching tools.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They also have to keep themselves abreast of industry, jobs and career trends.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Most of all, their hearts are in the right place.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Senior Career Coach Cheng Hing Nan can feel the pain and anxiety of jobseekers because he himself was retrenched before.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One client, Mr Wong, was an LTU whose previous salary was more than $10,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Career Coach Hing Nan knew Mr Wong was under immense stress and had low morale.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, he focused on the emotional well-being of Mr Wong.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He stayed in constant touch with him, checked on his family, helped him with industry research and also prepared him for interviews.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After six months of teamwork, Mr Wong found a job as a project manager with a local research facility.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It requires us to be sensitive and responsive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, we have to adopt a case approach, a very personal approach.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I salute our career coaches at WSG, e2i and our Career Centres for their passion, professionalism and their perseverance in serving our jobseekers one to one, one by one, day after day, with their heads and hearts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I urge them to press on because our work is never done.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to strengthen the inclusiveness of our local workforce to strengthen our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we also need to enhance the complementarity of our local and foreign workforce to enhance our economic competitiveness, a point made by Mr Lee Yi Shyan.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, the third key we need to have is the key of inclusiveness and complementarity.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: My colleague Minister of State Sam Tan will address our support for mature workers, low-wage workers and workers who have caregiving responsibilities at home.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I will share my thoughts on how we can manage better the inter-relationship between the local and foreign workforce in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One third of our Singapore workforce today is foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is a permanent feature because we can never be self-sufficient in having enough local workers, both in number and diversity of expertise.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Excluding foreign domestic workers (FDWs), we now have about 1.2 million foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Are they here to complement us, or to compete against us?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Forty percent, or about 450,000, of them take on labour-intensive jobs − construction, marine, process sectors – demanding jobs few locals want to do.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in the construction sector, they build our HDB flats, roads, Mass Rapid Transit networks and other amenities to make Singapore more liveable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Forty-five percent, about half a million, of them do jobs that locals want to do, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we do not have enough locals to do all these jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, PMETs − nurses, engineers, technicians; rank and file − cleaners, drivers, service staff.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, integrated circuit (IC) design is a highly specialised profession.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It requires minimally a Bachelor's degree in Electronics Engineering and half of them have postgraduate qualifications in IC design and microelectronics.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we do not have enough of them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Given the global shortage for such talent, having foreign IC Design Engineers here is a plus for us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They help us to support the growth of our industry and thereby create more such good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, we will continue to strengthen our Singaporean Core through MOE's Singapore Industry Scholarship and EDB's Industrial Postgraduate Programme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of the remaining 15%, those in global headquarters help bring jobs to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Global companies can locate their global headquarters anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having them here is good for our Singaporeans because for every three foreigners in our headquarters workforce, headquarters operations, there are about seven locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They also give Singaporeans more opportunities to be exposed to new job functions, international working environment and global best practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those in info-communications help to bring technical skills to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There are about more than 100 skills clusters that can be found in the info-communications industry in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Foreigners are stronger in some of these skills clusters than our locals, and likewise our locals are stronger in some of these skills clusters compared to the foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, together, they make us more globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the whole, most of the foreigners working in Singapore do complement our local workforce rather than substitute our locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Why then this persistent view that foreigners are here to take away our jobs?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I believe one reason is "pockets of concentration".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because in some companies, some segments of industries, some locations, the employers have not given fair consideration to the recruitment and development of our local manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What they have done is wrong, so we are taking actions against them, subject them to closer scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, I announced the implementation of a Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) Watchlist.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asked for an update on the FCF watchlist.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They come from various industries − ICT, professional services, financial and insurance activities, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Once placed on the FCF Watchlist, TAFEP guides them to improve their employment practices over a period of six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They stepped up local recruitment with the help of WSG and NTUC-e2i.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They collaborate with IHLs on the recruitment of new graduates.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They put in place inhouse programmes to groom our local talents and they facilitate know-how transfer to our locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If they continue to improve and adopt fair and progressive practices, they can progressively be removed from the watchlist.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, about 50 of them have not been receptive or cooperative.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have not seen enough improvement after six months of engagement with them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested that TAFEP be given more teeth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I want to emphasise that the vast majority of the employers are treating our locals fairly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We hope our action against these unfair employers will help reshape the local-foreign mindset for the better, from one of "2/3 versus 1/3" towards one of "2/3 and 1/3".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we move into the future economy, we need to go another step further, not just "2/3 versus 1/3" to "2/3 and 1/3", but towards a new mindset of "2/3 plus 1/3" can be bigger than one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are starting small with a select group of employers and their employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They come from different industries, from manufacturing to services, export-oriented and domestic bound, hi-tech and hi-touch.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They also belong to different types of enterprises − local enterprises and MNCs, Government-linked companies (GLCs) and SMEs, business enterprises and social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are very different enterprises, but they all share three same commitments.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked what are the criteria.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The criteria are that they must share three same commitments as everybody else.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This can be supported under the SkillsFuture Leadership Development initiative, a point made by Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Yvonne Lee joined the company eight years ago.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She and our local pioneer team learned from four foreign experts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They were also sent overseas for training exposure.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, in what is a traditionally male-dominated environment, Yvonne is now a Senior Manufacturing Director, leading a team of more than 300.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are based in Singapore and Austin, Texas.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the development of local talents has made the Singapore facility the global facility for a major series of equipment in Applied Materials.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are employers who engage in unfair HR practices with the mindset of "2/3 versus 1/3".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will send a clear message to all employers that foreign manpower is and will always be an integral part of our Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, we do expect and require all employers to give fair consideration to the recruitment and development of our local manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is not only the right thing to do for our people, but also the right thing to do for businesses for both to grow better in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Over the years, we have made major changes to our labour laws to cover more workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, Parliament passed the Employment Claims Act in August to resolve salary-related disputes, both statutory and contractual.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is especially helpful for PMEs who are not covered by the EA and have no access to the Labour Court, a point made by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I am also happy to share with the House that we have started a pilot since September last year to offer voluntary mediation for disputes that are outside the scope of ECT.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will build on this early success and progressively broaden the scope of services at TADM, again, a point made by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: TADM will also work with Law Society of Singapore to provide access to legal clinics.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Where skills upgrading or new employment is needed, TADM will partner WSG and e2i to help.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For those who require help with financial or socio-emotional issues, TADM will link them up with Social Service Offices and Family Service Centres respectively.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They can also find out more about services provided by the unions at TADM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And yet at the same time, more need to be done In our future economy, we will see higher proportion of PMETs; at the same time, rank-and-file workers will also become more skilful and professional.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the line between PMETs and rank-and-file will become less distinct in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As the employment profile of our workforce continues to evolve, our current framework of employment protection and workplace practices will need to evolve, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Not just the EA, the Industrial Relations Act and Trade Unions Act, which we will continue to review, but also tripartite mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay has made several suggestions to review our employment legislation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, employers may have their concerns and reservations, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to find the right balance and this is best done through tripartite consultations.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we will follow up with the suggestions made by Mr Patrick Tay and to engage NTUC and SNEF together to find a way forward.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, on one hand, we mandate basic workplace practices through laws and supplement them with tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Failure to comply can result in action by MOM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One example is the Retirement and Re-employment Act, and the Tripartite Guidelines on Re-employment of Older Employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Employers must comply when making Employment Assistance Payment (EAP).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Failing to do so can result in MOM taking actions against the employer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the other hand, we promote and encourage progressive work practices through tripartite advisories, for example, The Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It recommends companies to develop a harassment prevention policy on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked to mandate retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked whether we can make it more certain for employees to be entitled to retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The current approach, we believe, is a balanced one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, we will keep updating it but, right now, we think it is a balanced one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One limitation of our current approach is that there is a gap between the two: law and guidelines for compliance; and advisories for voluntary adoption.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Workers do not know exactly which employers are committed to adopt which progressive workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Likewise, progressive employers are not able to differentiate themselves and be known as fair and progressive employers to better attract talent.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The tripartite partners, therefore, decided to introduce what will be known as Tripartite Standards to complement the existing employment laws, tripartite guidelines and advisories.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Each standard will specify a set of progressive practices that are verifiable and can also be sector-specific.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, we can have a tripartite standard on FWAs or we can have one that specifies working arrangements in a specific sector like the media sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Employers can then make public their adoption of the standards through the Jobs Bank and TAFEP website.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Jobseekers would be able to identify these companies as employers of choice.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Taken together, laws, guidelines and standard advisories will form a comprehensive map to help employers build fair and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If Members know of any specific cases, they may refer them to TAFEP for investigation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those currently employed worry about losing their jobs, while the unemployed worry about when they can find a job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, when we talk about the new direction for future economic development, it is inevitable that people would have questions in their minds.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They wonder if job prospects would be more uncertain in the future and if there will be less job security.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Entrepreneurs in Singapore are also wondering, with so many difficulties in getting customers and workers, will it become increasingly difficult to conduct businesses and manufacturing operations?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I can assure our people that what we are trying to achieve for our nation and companies is not a slowing economy and employment market.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the contrary, through economic transformation, we want to strive for better business opportunities, better jobs, better prospects in the future economy and a better employment market.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In this fast-changing globalised economy, competition is stiff and survival hinges on creativity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To succeed and thrive, workers and companies must be highly-skilled and utilise technology fully.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the outset, it seems that utilising technology would reduce demand for workers, hence, it is not good for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, however, if we are able to adopt and make use of technology faster than other countries and companies to enhance our competitiveness, technology can improve how we work and help us do more and do better, then more and better opportunities will come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: All these will benefit our people as they enjoy better job opportunities and our SMEs will have even more opportunities and more room for development.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We all know that success does not come easily.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we run too slowly, we might lose our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we run too fast, some businesses and workers might lag behind.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we must be decisive and united, support one another and move forward together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When it comes to economic transformation, Singapore has never failed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Be it now or in the future, we will continue to be successful.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I, therefore, urge everyone to be confident and to have faith in the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Let us work together to strive for better jobs for our workers, better markets for businesses and a better future for our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: (In English): Madam, it was dark at night.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A man was looking for something under a bright lamp post.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A passerby asked: "Are you looking for something?" He said, "Yes, I am looking for my key." "How big is your key?" "This big." "Oh, that should be easy to find." So, the passerby joined in the search.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After five minutes, they found nothing. "Are you sure the key is this big?" He said, "Yes." "Are you sure you lost it here?" "No, no, no, over there, in the bushes." "Then, why are we searching for your key here?" "Because it is too dark over there." "It's brighter, it's easier to search here." Madam, many countries today face the problem of failure: problem with high and sticky unemployment, problem with wage stagnation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Not a problem of failure but challenges of success.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We got here because we did not take the easy way out: searching for lost key at the wrong place.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We had the courage to restructure when needed, continuously.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Most of all, we got here because our tripartite partnership is strong and our workers, our businesses, our people, they are good.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, working in unity, we are pro-worker, we are pro-business because, if one is weak, the others cannot be strong.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The two are either mutually reinforcing, like what we have here in Singapore, or mutually weakening, like what we see elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are not the only one trying to unlock the door to a future of good jobs and better careers, a future of fair and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many countries are searching for keys, too, but not many have succeeded.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some may have found one out of four, two out of four or even three out of four, but not four out of four.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, maybe these four keys are simply not there in the bushes in the first place.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is why instead of joining in the search for keys, whether in dark bushes or under a bright lamp post, we have always made our own keys to create our own future, the Singapore Tripartite Way.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, please have confidence in ourselves, in one another and in our future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First, I want to thank the Minister for the stories that resonate with us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It was created and performed by migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The protagonist, a migrant worker, knelt in front of his supervisor pleading not to be sent home because of a small injury.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In forum theatre, the audience would come up to enact solutions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A member of the audience, who is also a migrant worker, wanted to offer his.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then he knelt down and pleaded for forgiveness, which was the same as what happened in the original play.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, this migrant worker told his own story, the same story, and then he broke down on stage.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Foreign workers experience displacement that comes with high risk of life derailment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They come here to provide for their families and in the course of it, they also contribute to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many achieved their aims of a better life, but for no small numbers, things turned out badly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The derailment they suffer is quite often very severe because of two reasons.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First, the sunk cost of getting a job here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He desperately hopes that the Work Permit will be renewed for a few years.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Since he must avoid doing anything to jeopardise his job or displease his boss, the power relationship is severely distorted against the worker.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Even when bosses do not pay salaries for months, he may feel unable to protest too much or lodge complaints.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is where the second factor comes into play.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But if a worker lodges a complaint against his non-paying employer and loses his job, he will be sent home.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, if he wants another job, he has to pay an agent thousands of dollars again.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In any case, no worker contemplating lodging a complaint over salary non-payment will feel secure by relying on mere assurance of discretionary considerations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, I would urge the Ministry to review the policy requiring workers to be repatriated once an employer terminates the job.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge the Ministry to look at ways to eliminate recruitment costs to workers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I understand the South Korean government has, since 2004, begun operating a system that caps costs to workers to well under US$2,000, for contracts of up to five years.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It may be a model worth looking at.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Salary disputes between domestic workers and their employers often arise because there is no record to prove whether payments were made correctly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While local employment agencies are only allowed to collect a maximum of two months' salary as placement fees, domestic workers often have salary deductions that exceed this limit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These excessive deductions are often characterised as loan repayments for agency fees incurred in the worker's home country.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the lack of any records makes it difficult to determine if these deductions are legitimate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Electronic payments would help authorities to determine if workers are paid correctly and punctually and begin to throw some light on this problem of excessive salary deductions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Centre for Domestic Employees (CDE) has announced its intentions to push for electronic payment by General Interbank Recurring Order (GIRO) or bank transfer for domestic employees, which has also been welcomed by the Association for Employment Agencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share if there any plans to work with these two organisations in the implementation of such a scheme?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Minister Lim Swee Say mentioned the importance of strengthening the bridge of innovation so that more companies can transform and grow and successfully cross both the technology gate and market gate.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Companies which can do so will be better placed to tap on growth opportunities, contribute to our economic growth and create more quality jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Since its start in October 2015, when Minister Lim launched the Lean Enterprise Development Scheme (LEDS), to end-January 2017, LEDS had been "playing this bridge", the bridge of innovation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The vast majority, close to 90%, of the 2,100 companies were helped by some form of digitisation or technology adoption or, for some, it is just simply outsourcing.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This is how we are helping SMEs to go digital.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is not just the companies that have benefited from this, but workers have also benefited from improved productivity and technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I agree with Mr Chong Kee Hiong that success stories should be shared so that we can encourage more companies to come on board.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The example is "The Singapore Curry by Velu", a restaurant, a very small SME, implemented a very simple software solution to help them so that they can become less reliant on manpower.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Before the change, service crew either memorised or took down orders on paper, which is quite common if you go to some of the merchant shops or even the small restaurants.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With over 100 items on the menu, this conventional method was unproductive and also prone to errors as some orders were missed out and this affected customer service standards.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It was obvious that the restaurant needed some change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With support from NTUC-e2i and WSG, it introduced an integrated system to link up the ordering system with the point-of-sale (POS) system and the kitchen processing system.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, orders are now taken using tablets that relay the orders to the kitchen electronically, the service crew no longer need to memorise the orders or rush to the kitchen to relay the orders before they forget, and no orders will be missed out.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As a result, the business operations are now smoother.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Technology has also transformed jobs for workers and, most importantly, it has also changed the mindsets of workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Now, they treat technology as their co-worker and also as a friend instead of as a threat.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As he is 65, he does not know technology nor how to use a tablet computer until this change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, it is now easier for him to perform his service duties.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: He picked up the new skills, learning how to use technology, such as tablet computers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With greater confidence in using technology, he was also able to apply his newly acquired skills in his daily life, learning how to use the WhatsApp messenger to communicate with his grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As Mr Anwar improved his productivity and enhanced his skills − he has a good employer − his employer increased his salary by about 16%.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This example illustrates that when a company innovates and transforms to become more productive, jobs improve and the workers benefit as well through acquisition of new skills and higher wages.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is a win-win for both firms and workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Therefore, I fully support Mr Desmond Choo's very good suggestion to encourage firms which have received support for productivity improvement to share their gains with their workers, either in the form of higher wages or investment in their training.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Under LEDS, NTUC-e2i has already built in a wage increase requirement for supported workers − the IGP.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For all firms, whether under LEDS or not, subsidies, such as the substantial training subsidies and absentee payroll, are provided for companies to continue to invest in upgrading workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Nonetheless, we can do more to encourage productivity gains sharing.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We will explore this with the LEDS Taskforce agencies in the coming year, and that will be our main focus.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Jessica Tan asked how we are continuing our efforts to help more companies transform.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I have just described the benefits that can be derived or gained from a single company or a single enterprise transformation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But this year, our objective, our focus will be to provide or to push out cluster solutions, as Minister Lim had mentioned, for groups of companies, cluster of companies, sectors and the industry.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We want to make it as pervasive as possible.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: There were 30 preschool centres that have actually outsourced their backend kitchens to a single centralised kitchen and a solution.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We want to make sure that it is pervasive and nurture more industry cluster-based projects to create a viral effect in adopting some of the solutions, whether it is technology or just process redesign.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We will do this by supporting the development of "cluster" solutions that have been prequalified by IMDA and the sector agencies, such as SPRING Singapore, to be capable of driving productivity improvement, skills development and innovation across each industry.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: These include off-the-shelf technology and those solutions under the SMEs Go Digital Programme announced by the Minister for Finance in his Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The first solution is the one that can be adopted at the individual company level that can also be scaled up for industry-wide adoption by multiple firms.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is very simple and is from a company called Intercorp Solutions.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It uses highly precise facial biometric technology to capture and track real-time manpower utilisation, such as workers' attendance, working hours and productivity manhours spent onsite.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is a simple solution to use, off-the-shelf.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With this solution, companies no longer need to rely on the conventional way of tracking manpower utilisation onsite by marking workers' attendance manually.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For smaller companies, they can actually self-register through the system.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This reduces the administrative burden on the operational staff so that they can spend more time on other higher value jobs.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: In addition, this management system allows users to generate detailed comprehensive graphical reports from the captured workforce data that they can use to enhance their operations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For example, project managers can use the reports to understand manpower utilisation onsite and improve the operational efficiency with better manpower planning and allocation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The second solution is a shared-service solution that can be adopted by many manufacturing companies concurrently.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is an online B2B Industrial Excess Marketplace from Excess Inventory Guru Pte Ltd that provides a cloud-based platform for manufacturing companies to manage their online sale of excess inventory and automate some of their tedious and manual business operations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For this year's economic climate, this may be an important software platform for many companies out there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This is a good solution that can help manufacturing companies save carrying costs and also help them achieve a leaner backend operation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: These are just two of many prequalified solutions that have proven effective.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Our objective is to accelerate adoption of these solutions, not just having one or two more companies doing this, but from "Addition to Multiplication", from individual firms to cluster- or industry-wide adoption.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We know that this is not an easy task.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We need to have a lot of handholding and encouragement to encourage the companies to come forward.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We are going to adopt a three-pronged approach: engagement, access and support for faster development.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong would be pleased to know that we will step up efforts to outreach through our network of 18 LEDS multipliers to reach out to more companies and industries.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Roadshows will be organised, and more of them will be organised, for relevant prequalified solution providers to showcase their solutions to the companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The LEDS Taskforce will also work even closer with industries, especially those that have lesser companies applying to LEDS or undergoing the Lean Management Change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: They can be in the hospitality, landscape and cleaning industries, which are those that we hope to encourage more to move up the productivity index.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We will also work with the relevant agencies that are championing some of the other sectors to push out more solutions to the companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Second, we must continue to give companies ready access to all these prequalified solution providers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The spirit of LEDS is for "One Stop Service" because we will bring all of our schemes and grants between the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and MOM together.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Companies which are willing to transform need only take the first step − approach any of the LEDS agencies or our LEDS partners, SME centres inclusive, or they can also approach NTUC-e2i and the TACs, and we will take them through this journey and link them up with these solution providers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: To accelerate adoption, we are prepared to grant the prequalified solution providers and the solutions that are provided by these companies, temporary manpower support under LEDS.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We want to scale up and help to ramp up this solution towards the sector.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Our position is very simple – we hope that LEDS can not only transform a company but strengthen the sector as well, so that more quality jobs can be created.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: They take on demanding jobs that few locals want to do and jobs where there is a shortage of local workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I agree with Mr Kok Heng Leun that we should ensure that our foreign workers are treated fairly and provided with good working conditions.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Of course, it saddens me to hear such a story being related and we are continuously trying to tighten our process to make sure our migrant workers are protected.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This would include ensuring that they have safe workplaces as well, and also that they receive their due salaries and get compensated if they are injured on their job.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, not all foreign workers want that, because sometimes when you talk to them, they may not want to change employers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: They may just prefer to return home after their claim is resolved.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, we need to have a lot of consultation and work with the workers as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Mr Kok mentioned about the Korean system and the issues with recruitment cost.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But we constantly learn from other countries and that will include the Korean system as well, and we will review and study it further.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: In the unfortunate event of an accident, employers must additionally take care of their injured workers, help them recover from their injuries and assist them to return to work quickly.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: When applying for or renewing the work passes of their foreign workers, employers are required to provide insurance policy details to MOM.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Moving forward, MOM will step up efforts to ensure that the policies remain valid throughout the worker's work duration in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We will also want to educate and reach out and remind employers on the need to maintain insurance coverage for their workers during their stay.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We will partner the General Insurance Association of Singapore and the Singapore Contractors Association Ltd on this front.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Similarly, it is every employer's responsibility to ensure that salaries are paid on time.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Where employers willfully refuse to comply with the law to pay the salaries due to their workers, MOM will take such employers to task.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, beyond punitive enforcement action against such employers, we should ensure that, in the meantime, foreign workers are provided with adequate assistance.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: In this case, my Ministry works closely with the Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC).

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Foreign workers who approach MOM on housing or other subsistence issues will receive timely assistance from MOM and our partners like MWC.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: MWC has been helping foreign workers with various employment issues since 2009.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Such assistance includes providing housing and subsistence to workers in need, as well as advising and assisting the workers on the enforcement of Labour Court orders.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: In some cases, foreign workers have been provided with an ex-gratia payment if the prospects of recovering the monies were slim.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As an example, MWC has been helping two Bangladeshi foreign workers who were badly burnt in a serious workplace accident since January this year.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: MWC has been working closely with like-minded partners like Silver Ribbon and Healthserve, as well as the hospital, to provide emotional, psychological and physical support to the workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As the employer has exhausted his finances helping the workers, MWC stepped in to provide the workers with housing and financial assistance for the payment of additional surgery through the Fund.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: To better help foreign workers in need, MWC will set up a new office − it is an additional office − to be co-located with the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) at the MOM Service Centre.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This is in addition to their two offices, as I mentioned, and the other two offices are in Serangoon and Geylang.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Foreign workers who need help can approach MWC at any of these three locations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Besides having a safe working environment, it is also important that foreign workers return to a clean and safe accommodation after a hard day's work.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: These standards ensure foreign workers have access to a cleaner and safer accommodation with amenities.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is exactly the reason why we implemented the Foreign Employees Dormitories Act (FEDA) from 1 January last year to regulate large dormitories that house 1,000 or more workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With the higher standards required under FEDA, foreign workers in licensed large dormitories are assured of safe and well-maintained living spaces.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: As announced in August 2016, factory-converted dormitories (FCDs), which are smaller, will also have to meet additional conditions, not just meeting the minimum standards but some additional conditions, including personal lockers to workers, and establishing a feedback mechanism and the installation of wi-fi.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And for many, before we even come up with the additional conditions, they have already implemented them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: On FDWs, Mr Louis Ng asked if MOM had plans to support the CDE and employment agencies in their push for electronic payment of salaries for domestic workers as proof of salary payment in the event of a dispute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This tripartite code or standards will be an important step to further companies' commitment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I also suggest that these standards come attached with incentives for abiding by the standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Employees in companies where there is such a standard have a right to FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We can also consider implementing this sectorally, starting with those where technology-enabled FWA can be made more pervasive, such as the banking, accounting and ICT sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Participating companies in the Human Capital Partnership Programme should also commit to these tripartite standards.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Going to work may not necessarily mean that one has to physically travel to an office or workplace and stay there for a prescribed number of hours in order to be seen to be working.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The use of technologies, mobile applications and social media has allowed individuals to offer their products and services and manage their clients or buyers at their own time and according to their own targets.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If employers are not quick enough to leverage technology and offer FWAs for their employees, they risk losing these employees to freelance work, which also allows these employees to fulfil personal or family responsibilities, such as caregiving or raising their families.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: On top of that, there is a largely untapped pool of human resource among our stay-at-home mothers and retirees who are able to be a part of our workforce.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What they need is a buffer period to transit back to work and learn relevant work skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: My fellow Members of Parliament, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Desmond Choo, have spoken about this before and I have proposed a returnship programme.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How can our Ministry help employers implement progressive work practices or FWAs to help different segments of Singaporeans remain economically active and yet fulfil personal responsibilities, such as caregiving or raising their families?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How can women and economically active retirees who are going back to the workforce be helped through FWAs, where they can ease back into full-time positions over a reasonable period of time and learn relevant new skills, so that they are not left behind?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: In addition, how can rank-and-file or blue-collar workers learn relevant skills so that they are employable and can avail themselves of more employment opportunities and not be competing with new technologies at the workplace?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It makes sense to help our older workers stay active in the workplace for longer if they so choose.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: When we make it possible for older workers to remain active in the workforce as they wish, we help them contribute to their own economic and social well-being.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In addition, their fellow workers and society in general also benefit from the full utilisation of their human capital.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Employers can help their older workers become more effective workers in their jobs by redesigning the workplace, work processes and even the job itself.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Last year saw several Government initiatives in the area.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Also last year, a programme was launched to offer an array of courses for companies and individuals on age management at the workplace − a programme administered by the Singapore Institute of Management (UniSIM), in collaboration with MOM and others.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: These Government initiatives focus on efforts for Job Redesign for Older Workers at the enterprise level and they are welcomed.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry look into making these efforts also at the industry level?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This is because while workplaces and processes may be particular to a company, different companies in the same industry share a great deal in common.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, resources could be pooled by companies in the industry to develop best practices, to modify tools and equipment for use off-the-shelf by older workers throughout the industry.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, Job Redesign for Older Workers could be identified as a key component of each ITM currently being developed across the economy.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, Job Redesign for Older Workers can be set out among the suite of initiatives for improving productivity in any given industry.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We know productivity is one of the four pillars supporting the growth and competitiveness plans of any given ITM.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Another way to envision Job Redesign for Older Workers as a key component of ITMs may be to think of it as a third horizontal, along with promoting ICT adoption and skills development, which can help to support the ITMs and produce improvements across the economy in the face of an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: An article on Cable News Network (CNN) caught my attention a few weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It tells the story about a hotel in a hikers' paradise in West Scotland.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The foreign workers there were promised specific jobs with decent salaries.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But when they arrived, job scopes were limitless, working hours were endless and pay was meagre.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The boss demanded additional payments from these workers to sponsor their visa, threatened to cancel their work permit if they do not cooperate, and warned them about arrest and deportation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The owner of the hotel is now serving time for labour trafficking for a group of men from Bangladesh.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Modern slavery is happening everywhere, possibly exacerbated by globalisation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: You can see modern slaves working in the heart of our estates.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These foreign cleaners work late into the night, seven days a week with no rest day and low wages.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They even work when they were injured or sick.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They have to work non-stop because they are living in bondage.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The mathematics and the easy money are just too tempting for some people to pass up.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Foreign workers are reluctant to come forth with their story for fear of losing their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Many of them sold their possessions and borrowed heavily to come here to make a living.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They have huge debts to pay and, at the same time, hungry mouths to feed back home.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Coming out against their employers will mean losing their jobs and everything, a risk they can ill-afford to take.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The master of the modern slave trade knows this fear very well, and they milk these workers to the maximum.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have seen cases of local cleaners working without payslips or contracts.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For some, their payslips comprise unexplained or unjustified deductions.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some are given payslips with no CPF contributions stated and they do not know why.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some are not sure about their basic employment benefits, but they dare not confront their employers for fear of losing of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these local cleaners are elderly and illiterate and their next job may be hard to come by.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is hard to imagine that despite all the education, publicity and threat of prosecution, such practices still persist.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Collectively, the Town Councils in Singapore hire a substantial number of cleaners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I told my General Manager to inform the cleaning contractors in Hougang I do not want such practices to surface in the estate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am helped by warm-hearted residents who will not stand for any abuse of cleaners in their neighbourhood as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The cleanliness of our estate cannot come at the expense of the misery of the cleaners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is time for us to clean up the cleaning industry for a change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The last time this figure was revised was in 2013.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: While the four changes made to enhance the scheme were welcome and necessary, would increasing the cash component not provide a far more direct reward for work effort?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Increasing the cash component would allow workers to benefit immediately from the fruits of their labour and be a source of motivation to strive harder to improve their quality of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This way, they could get promoted and improve their earnings, which is a more effective and encouraging way to help low-income workers build up retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is to improve the employment benefits and job security to attract younger workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It also protects them from the wage fluctuations or resetting that is very common for workers in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC would like to seek the Government's support in this endeavour, the same way it had given its support to the revision for the cleaning PWM.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, can future reviews of WIS eligibility take into consideration the review done on PWM and maybe, in particular, to consider increasing the salary eligibility criterion.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In doing so, I believe we would be going one step closer to ensuring fairer equity for these workers so that they may enjoy the fruits of Singapore's economic growth.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SRF was set up by SLF in response to the 1978 Spyros accident to provide financial assistance to industrial accident victims and their families while they awaited Workmen's Compensation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, SRF is co-administered by MOM and SLF, with MOM screening the applications and SLF disbursing payments based on MOM's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC would like to propose for the administration of the funds to be reviewed to reflect the core purpose of the fund and to benefit low-wage workers by raising the income eligibility criterion.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, as U Care Centre was set up to better serve low-wage workers, perhaps MOM could consider letting U Care Centre to be the fund administrator.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must do more to improve our workplace safety and health standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, there are many workgroups formed to tackle workplace safety and health at the sectoral level, the functional level and even workgroups targeting at the cause of injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To enable smooth implementation of initiatives at the working level, can there be better coordination among and across different workgroups?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, the Ministry issued a guide to encourage companies to report "near misses".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A "near miss" is often seen as a narrow escape, a stroke of luck.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the benefits of a systematic recording of "near misses" may help to prevent a recurrence, identify any weaknesses in operational procedures and, when reviewed over a period of time, may allow us to detect patterns which could potentially prevent future fatalities, especially in high-risk industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry do more to encourage "near miss" reporting?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, I must also caution that it would be counter intuitive to penalise companies and workers who report "near misses".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Instead, more guidance should be provided to these companies to prevent future possible accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry organise industry-specific forums or create platforms to allow companies to share "near misses"?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry also consider incentivising and rewarding companies with good "Design for Safety" concept and implementation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second "C" is the need for greater commitment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Be it top management, ground supervisors or workers, we all have a part to play in ensuring workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a need for greater commitment and ownership across all levels to collectively help raise workplace safety and health standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For a start, we can consider the 1-2-3 approach.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Government also consider awarding contracts only to bizSAFE-accredited companies for major infrastructure projects?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The third "C" is to adopt a more targeted coaching to raise awareness of safe workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While there is a need to raise standards across the board, we should also focus more attention on the top three − the top three industries with the most fatalities; and the three most common incident types.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry consider implementing a mentoring scheme between bizSAFE-accredited company and other non-accredited companies within the same industry?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A targeted approach would be more relevant as it addresses specific risks inherent to the industry and the sharing of experiences and best practices among similar industry players would certainly be more useful.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, only a fraction of employers proactively help their injured employees during and after the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some workers may find it hard to return to their original jobs while others may even lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry establish a scheme to better help injured workers get back to work?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This scheme should include a structured case management system to help our workers with injury management, rehabilitation, job redesign, job placement and even work injury compensation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we want to build a genuine culture of care for our workers' well-being or do we want to adopt a strategy of punitive measures to force employers to comply with safety regulations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we prefer to see the light or feel the heat?

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will do more for our older workers, low-wage workers and workers with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: To encourage employers to voluntarily re-employ older workers not covered by the new re-employment age, the Government has extended the Additional Special Employment Credit to incentivise employers to do so.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In addition, it is equally important to ensure that workplaces are age-friendly to meet the needs of our older workers and also help them to stay productive.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Employers must play their part in this aspect.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Chen Show Mao asked about the progress of workplace and job redesign for our older workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In 2013, we introduced WorkPro to support companies to develop age-friendly workplaces and make jobs for our older workers easier, safer and smarter.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: WorkPro was enhanced in July last year with more generous funding.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Besides increased funding, companies from all industries can also tap on the Job Redesign toolkit and clinics to improve their knowledge about job redesign.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: More employers have since taken up the WorkPro Job Redesign Grant.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Over the last seven months, 103 companies have tapped on this grant.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: More than 1,800 older workers aged 50 and above stand to benefit from the enhanced WorkPro.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The hotel obtained WorkPro funding to replace the standard tables in their restaurant with a multi-purpose table called Livecookingtable that can be used as a cooker, warmer or even cooler.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Au Tiang Kok is one of the older workers who have benefited from this change.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In his job, Mr Au is responsible for the setting up and clearing of buffet trays at the restaurant.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: These buffet trays with burners weighed around 30 kilogrammes each.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: It was a very heavy and laborious job for Mr Au.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: With the Livecookingtable, the restaurant now uses a different type of buffet trays without burners.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: These new trays are lighter to carry, and Mr Au is no longer at risk of getting burnt by the open flame.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I am heartened to know that 67-year-old Mr Au is happy with this job redesign and he intends to continue working to contribute meaningfully for as long as he can.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Au's story tells us that the commitment of management is important.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I am, therefore, glad that the HR Director, Mr Francis Tan, believes strongly in job redesign and makes use of technology to improve older workers' productivity.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: During the Budget Debate, Mr Heng Chee How spoke passionately about the need for older workers to continue to adapt and grow while companies transform and grow.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I agree fully with Mr Heng that older workers must continually upskill, reskill and deepskill to enhance their employability.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Skills upgrading is the best safeguard for workers during this period of economic and job transformation.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Older workers should also take advantage of the various Government training schemes available, such as SkillsFuture, to enhance their employability.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Over the last five years, incomes of full-time employed Singapore Citizens at the 20th percentile grew by 3.2% per annum in real terms.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This has kept pace with the 3.1% annualised growth in real median incomes of our employed citizens over the same period.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: To continue our efforts to uplift our low-wage workers, we adopt a three-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Currently, companies' entitlement to foreign workers is based on the dependency ratio ceiling.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: For example, a dependency ratio ceiling of 60% in the manufacturing sector means that the employer can hire up to 1.5 foreign workers for every one full-time equivalent local worker hired.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: A local worker who earns a monthly salary of $1,000 or above is considered a full-time equivalent.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We review this salary threshold regularly to stay in line with rising income trends.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We expect that low-wage workers' wages will adjust in line with the new threshold.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We last reviewed the threshold in 2013, that was about four years ago.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The 10th percentile income then was already $1,200 and had risen to $1,300 in 2015.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, if we do not update the salary threshold now, it will mean having to make an even larger increase in future.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Another way to support wage increases is through PWM, which is mandatory in the cleaning, security and landscaping sectors.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The PWMs have helped more than 70,000 resident workers in these sectors grow their wages.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Before the introduction of the cleaning PWM, median gross wages for full-time resident cleaners grew by 2% per annum from 2009 to 2012.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, I thank Mr Zainal Sapari for his suggestions on incorporating annual increments and annual bonuses in the security and landscape PWMs.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: As Mr Zainal has pointed out, we have already done this for the cleaning sector.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The cleaning sector sets out annual adjustments to the PWM wage levels from this year up to 2022.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The Tripartite Cluster for Cleaners also encourages cleaning companies to provide increments to better performing workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This will raise their salaries to be above the PWM wage levels and still within the recommended salary range of their job rungs.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The security and landscape sectors only implemented PWMs recently in 2016.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We need to give them time to evolve, progress and improve.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: However, I still want to take this opportunity to encourage the tripartite committees in these sectors to learn from the cleaning sector and enhance their PWM commitments over time.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I also encourage employers and unions in other sectors to adopt the PWM concept, which brings together wages, skills and productivity to create meaningful career ladders for their workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: It will provide new guidance on supporting progressive remuneration and benefits for outsourced workers, as well as fair contracting practices.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM has worked closely with the Ministry of Finance (MOF) to ensure that all Government agencies support the updated Advisory.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Today, the Government procures cleaning and security services from accredited cleaning businesses and well-graded security agencies.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: These accreditation and grading frameworks take into account the progressive employment practices of these companies.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM is working with MOF, the Singapore Police Force, the National Environment Agency and the National Parks Board (NParks) to review further measures against contractors that fail to safeguard basic employment rights of outsourced workers working under Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: More details will be announced at a later stage.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: When Government agencies outsource many activities, Government contracts still make up only a small fraction of the total market for outsourced services.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, I want to urge tripartite committees, like the one chaired by Mr Zainal Sapari for the cleaning sector, to reach out to more private sector buyers to adopt best sourcing.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: My Ministry stands ready to work with the Labour Movement and employers to increase adoption of the Tripartite Advisory on Best Sourcing Practices.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Png Eng Huat asked about our efforts to protect foreign and local conservancy workers from unfair treatment and abuse.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: If they feel that they are unfairly treated, they should approach MOM or their unions for assistance or, at the minimum, they can approach the MWCs, CDE, NGOs and voluntary welfare organisations for assistance.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Third, we will continue to supplement the incomes and retirement savings of low-wage workers through WIS.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh proposed several changes to the WIS scheme.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: They were announced at last year's Budget and implemented since January this year.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Third, we will make more frequent WIS payouts, from quarterly to monthly, starting from March 2017, that is, this month.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This provides a more direct and timely reward for work effort.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Aside from helping them meet their immediate needs, WIS payouts are intended to help low-wage workers meet their basic retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is why WIS payouts comprise 40% cash and 60% CPF.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Raising the cash component and reducing the CPF component, as suggested by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, will mean workers will have less to set aside for retirement, and may not be able to meet the basic needs in old age.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We think that this may not be a wise approach.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Notwithstanding this, the Government already provides other grants and transfers, such as the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Vouchers, Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) rebates, WIS and so on, to top up low-wage workers' salaries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, taking all these together, this is already quite a substantial increase in the low-wage workers' income.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: While the cash component of WIS remains at 40% but, in actual terms, low-wage workers receive more cash with all the other social transfers from the Government.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will periodically review the WIS scheme to ensure that it continues to support the bottom 20% to 30% of our workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: More employers are now adopting FWAs, such as flexi-time, flexi-place and flexi-load.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In 2016, about two in three, or 67%, of the employees worked in firms that offered formal FWAs.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is up from just half, or 56%, in 2011.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: More than eight in 10 employees or, to be precise, 82% worked in firms that offer ad-hoc FWAs.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is up from seven in 10 in 2011.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Dr Intan, Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Desmond Choo asked about our efforts in promoting FWAs, especially for people with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, we looked at the employment rate of local women who continue to shoulder many caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We are already among the top in terms of full-time employment of females aged between 25 and 64, compared to all the other Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Conversely, Singapore's part-time employment is lower than that of most OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: While we are doing reasonably well, there is still room to improve the employment of our female residents, especially in the area of part-time employment.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We can do this through flexi-load options, such as "job sharing".

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Such options are important because they give caregivers an option to reduce or adjust their workload so that they can better manage their multiple responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Today, nearly all PMETs are on full-time employment, but they can still benefit from job sharing, which offers more choices to both PMETs and employers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Job sharing may come with some hand-over and coordination issues, but employers should think of ways to overcome them and make necessary adjustments and arrangements to promote greater job sharing in their companies.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
