text: Among them, 42 fatalities occurred in the first half of the year.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This improvement continued into the first two months of 2017 with two fatalities, as compared to 10 fatalities in the same period last year.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: However, to us, every fatality is still one tragedy that can be prevented.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: And every life lost is still one too many.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, we should remain vigilant and do more to make our workplaces safer and healthier for our workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Melvin Yong also asked what more can we do to reduce the number of workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: While it has improved from 2015, there are still three areas of concern that we will step up our actions and focus on.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: One is vehicular-related accidents within worksites; two, accidents involving formwork; and three, lack of proper supervision, coordination and communication of work activities resulting in accidents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will enhance the WSH Construction Regulations to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: To raise overall WSH performance, we need everyone to take greater WSH ownership.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Many progressive companies in Singapore already pay close attention to WSH.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In fact, nearly half of them discussed WSH issues regularly at their management meetings.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We should encourage more to do so, and we will consider laying out in the WSH Act clear roles for corporate officers in maintaining an effective WSH management system in their companies.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM investigators will also probe deeper into the role of companies' senior management in ensuring compliance.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: First, we should ensure that the injured workers, particularly the low-wage workers, receive additional financial support when needed.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Zainal Sapari had proposed to review the criteria and administration for the Singapore Labour Foundation Special Relief Fund (SRF) to benefit more low-wage workers who are victims of industrial accidents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Today, other than SRF, local injured workers can also obtain financial assistance under ComCare.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Nonetheless, we will work with our tripartite partners, including Mr Zainal Sapari, to review the usage and administration of SRF to provide injured workers with the assistance they require.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: At the same time, we should also help our injured workers return to work quickly.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Today, over 80% of injured workers are already able to return to work, and we want to do more to help them recover faster and also to return to work earlier.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This will also benefit employers who are able to retain their experienced employees and save on rehiring and retraining new employees.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how we are helping injured workers return to work.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This programme provides early intervention to help injured workers and their companies through personalised case management, a point mentioned by Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: RTW coordinators will facilitate injured workers to return to their workplaces early.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This includes helping employers to make adjustments to their workplaces and jobs to facilitate the injured worker's rehabilitation and return to work.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The tripartite partners will also be working together to implement the RTW programme later this year.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will share more details when it is worked out.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: However, it must be a national effort with the tripartite partners, employers and workers all playing their part together so that we will be able to grow our workplaces to make them inclusive and progressive.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: I wish to echo their concerns and reiterate the importance.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Currently, employment-related laws in Singapore, such as the EA, the CPF Act and WICA, outline the rights and responsibilities of employees and employers, including contributions towards housing, retirement and medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Unlike an employee, a freelancer performing work under a contract for service currently falls outside the scope of many provisions of our employment-related laws.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: I hope it will lead to the Government looking into extending to freelancers more of the protection currently afforded employees under our employment-related laws.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Perhaps, also to consider risk-pooling mechanisms yielding protection for freelancers in the event of work injury.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancing work is becoming an attractive option either on a full-time, part-time or project basis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aided by the emergence of the "sharing economy" platforms, this work has become more feasible for many.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While freelancers do have some flexibility of time, they face concerns, such as an unstable income stream, inadequate savings for retirement and, sometimes, lack of protection when disputes between them and the service buyer occur.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, I believe, will help us tackle the issues surrounding freelancers in a targeted manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have myself seen how the Minister for Manpower act on his concerns or the needs of low-wage workers, PMEs, foreign workers, including conservancy workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He has put in place laws to be enforced, jobs that are redesigned, contracts that are best sourced, and machinery put in place to help the work of, for example, conservancy workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, the cases highlighted earlier by Mr Png Eng Huat about modern slaves in the conservancy work is a very serious one.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because if there are such cases, they should be highlighted to MOM to be investigated and action taken against those employers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope those cases will be surfaced to MOM and action taken.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask the Manpower Minister how his team will go about gathering views of the freelancer communities and aggregators to identify their freelancing concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be focus group and feedback channels?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the Minister's own concerns pertaining to the challenges facing freelancers?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You control the time you spend, when you want to work, what you want to work on.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the gig economy, people may end up like rolling stones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They do not gather any moss − the opportunity to learn new skills will be absent as they are engaged in their prevailing skillset.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Job security is also sometimes non-existent and benefits non-existent as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Being your own boss, only by name, still means having to take full responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One key element of the employer and employee relationship in Singapore is CPF.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Housing, healthcare, education, retirement, all key pillars of our social policy link back to the CPF and to employment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While it may seem advantageous to be your own boss, employers also see great benefits, too, and we may see a race to the bottom and a shattering of our key social policy ideals.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I had then asked if the Ministry would investigate if benefits due to younger Singaporeans on temporary employment, freelance work or what we call perma-temps, as well as now in the gig economy, are being curtailed as they are not fully covered under employment-related laws.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Minister had replied then that feedback from the industry and unions would be sought.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I welcome, therefore, the most recent survey and the details that the Ministry will be able to provide.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This year's MOM focus is also about greater retirement adequacy and progressive work practices.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, the gig workers, freelancers and contract workers should not be allowed to fall through the cracks, as the gig economy continues to develop.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A disruptive economy is to be welcomed, but one that disrupts the very core of social policies in our country and Singaporeans must be one that we approach cautiously and carefully.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This also reflects the discussions I have had on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not just the much talked about millennial generation seeking a better work-life balance, there are many trends and larger forces at work pushing our economy in that direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we, as a House, need to ensure that our workers are adequately prepared for this eventuality to thrive in this new economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are covered by the policy as long as you work for the company.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From my own experience, once you stop working for the company, you are not covered anymore, even though you might want to pay up for it, and paying more in premium terms.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the old days, when people tended to stay in one job for many years, this might not be such a big deal.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But if you accept that people are going to be moving around in the new gig economy or entering into alternative work arrangements which fall short of full-time employment, then this limitation becomes a matter of concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It means, for example, that if you develop a condition in your current job, it will be considered a pre-existing condition.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When you sign up for an insurance policy in your new job, chances are that you might not be able to get it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You cannot get it at all because of your pre-existing condition; so, you cease to be covered.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The crucial point is that for many reasons, people change employment, moving from one job to another, becoming self-employed, retiring or being laid off.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All these scenarios will cause the worker to give up his current employer-paid insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the long run, experts believe that the solution will lie towards a move to a more individual-centric insurance system, instead of a company-centric one.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An interim solution would be to encourage the portability of company medical insurance benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened to see that we are already moving in that direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But at the moment, these are voluntary and seem to focus on the very basic insurance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the employee were to buy himself under an individual policy, he pays $1,000.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the company buys it under the company group insurance policy, and with risk-pooling, the cost might be $800.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The company is not disadvantaged in any way.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry can share if it has any plans, as part of a broader move towards a future-ready benefits system.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the new economy, the "gig economy" is gaining momentum and the attention of policymakers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Gig workers are those who perform contract-based, on-demand work.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many reports on "gig workers" have focused on job insecurity and significant social safety risks to a rapidly growing segment of workers, as we just heard from my colleagues.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But, with the right set of policy interventions, I believe it can also be the formula for higher workforce participation because of the benefits this FWA brings to both employers and employees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The gig economy may offer women with caregiving responsibilities and older workers who need more flexible work schedules the balance they are looking for.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, organise a marketplace that enables gig workers to access pooled medical coverage, also a marketplace that enables efficient job matching, where workers and employers rate each other.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, provide a special track in SkillsFuture for gig workers, so that they, too, can stay relevant and future-proof their skills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Fourth, quite importantly, prevent tax leakages arising from informal work arrangements and the creation of an underground economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the right set of policy measures, we can make this unstoppable trend of gig economy work for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the slew of enhancements made in 2015 to CPF has made it more attractive and flexible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged by the improved outreach efforts by CPF Board to increase members' awareness and understanding so they can receive the full benefits of the CPF scheme at different stages of their lives.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Enhancements include newly designed statements with bold graphics to aid comprehension, so they look very nice in multi-media outreach programmes and CPF Mobile Service Centres.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I hope these have helped members better optimise their savings and those of their family members.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister to share the recent trends the CPF board has observed, including how enquiries and transaction patterns of CPF accounts have changed, the topping up of members' accounts or those of unemployed family members, and how members choose between the various CPF LIFE Plans, that is, Basic, Full and Enhanced retirement sums.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Can the Minister give us an update on how CPFIS will be revamped to make it serve members better?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What is the design and timeline for the launch of LRIS so that members can benefit from a simpler investment option?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of our 30- to 40-something-year-old working professionals already take seriously the call to upskill or be left behind.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly true of those who are founders and entrepreneurs running small to medium-sized private sector or people sector organisations.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us founders hit our skill ceilings as our organisations scale from small to medium to large and, at each inflection point, many of us quickly realise that the only way to survive is to get exposed to worldclass level training and mentorship to keep our organisations resilient and relevant.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I ask working professionals and organisation founders online for examples of what courses some of them would definitely go for, if they could use their CPF to do so.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For some for them, the problem that gets in the way of going for such learning courses is simply liquidity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A white-collar working professional, especially 30- to 40-something-year-old founders and entrepreneurs heading their own small to medium organisations, can face surprising crunches in both personal and organisational resources.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some may find themselves caught between having to provide financial support for ageing parents and young children, while having to put in significant personal resources to support their own organisations during a long economic crunch.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, paying for their own personal learning is sometimes a struggle and put off as the last priority.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, there are cases of potential founders at a crucial peak of their leadership development period who put off going for training not because they do not think it is important or urgent, but they simply cannot spare liquidity for the moment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of them are definitely not looking for a handout from the Government, but they would like access to more liquidity, especially from their own resources.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the CPF Education Scheme was originally designed around members of lower-income families who want to further their education but did not have the liquidity to do so.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This will be really helpful for professionals in the people sector organisations, social enterprises and SMEs which do have less resources to tap on than professionals working for large public sector or private sector organisations who are better able to tap on their companies' sponsored learning.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Over the years, our CPF system has served Singaporeans well in supporting the retirement, housing and healthcare needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With wage growth and higher labour force participation rate, especially among older workers, we can expect CPF balances to keep improving in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A member who is 40 years old earning $6,000 a month will save $370 more a month.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And with interest, it will grow to $149,000 by the age of 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If a person continues working from 40 to 65 years old earning about $6,000 a month, it will add another $149,000 into his CPF account by the age of 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also helping older workers to save more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Another one million CPF members aged 55 and above, benefited from an additional extra interest of 1% on their first $30,000 savings in CPF.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For an older worker earning the median salary of $3,400 from age 50 to 65, the increase in CPF contribution and additional extra interest of 1% will add $14,000 to his retirement savings by the time he turns 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, we have also made it easier for members to transfer CPF savings to their spouses' account.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is an area that Ms Foo Mee Har is always concerned about.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They need to set aside only the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) instead of the Full Retirement Sum (FRS).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: About 2,700 members did some transfer and this is 70% more than the year before.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, the number of members who did transfer to their spouses has increased.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And about one-third of the increase was due to enhancements in our rules.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, one in five of the spouses who received transfers now have at least BRS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We also saw more cash top-ups last year to their own accounts or for their family members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More members are now doing cash top-ups, either for themselves or for their family members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Beyond BRS and FRS, we introduced the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And those with ERS at age 55 will receive $1,900 per month for life when they reach the withdrawal age of 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last but not least, CPF members also now have the option of deferring the starting age of their CPF LIFE payouts up to the age of 70.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They do not have to start at 64, even though the payouts' eligibility age is 64.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If they want to, they can defer to the age of 70.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, about 900 CPF LIFE members did that and about 70% are still working.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Half of them would have received payouts of more than $500 per month and they will all receive higher payouts by starting later.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr William Wong turned 65 years old just last week.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CPF LIFE, he would have received about $500 a month for life but Mr Wong chooses to defer his payout for as long as he is healthy and working.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, if he defers till 70 years old, his payout would increase to $680, instead of $500; an increase of about $180 per month, for life.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the whole, these recent CPF changes help both the younger and the older members to save more for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I hope more members will make good use of these options to meet their own needs better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked whether we could allow members to use their CPF savings for overseas training courses because, as she put it, some of these training courses are just too expensive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But in fact, it is for the same reason, why we are hesitating.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With a longer lifespan, we are doing more to safeguard member's retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to be careful about expanding the use of CPF for other expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we have no plans to open up the CPF Education Scheme for overseas programmes.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But let me emphasise that, in fact, I do agree with Ms Kuik that upgrading is very important.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is not that we are not supportive of upgrading but skills upgrading or professional upgrading is not one of the main purposes of CPF.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Upgrading is important but CPF savings is a wrong channel; not the right one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The CPF Advisory Panel observed that CPFIS is not designed for members who lack the time and knowledge to manage their own investments.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There is nothing wrong with the idea of the CPFIS investment scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But you must be in the right profile of investors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If you have the time, the knowledge, CPFIS is the right scheme for you.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But if you have no time and knowledge, then CPFIS may not be the best scheme for you.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, it could be better off for those who have no time and knowledge to leave their CPF money to earn the risk-free CPF interest rates.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To better serve the interest of CPF members, we are working on three areas of improvement to CPFIS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, the introduction of a self-assessment tool to help members to determine for themselves whether CPFIS is suitable for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we will provide a self-assessment tool for the CPF members to assess themselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the end of the test or assessment, if they still decide to proceed to invest through CPFIS, even though the self-assessment tool helps them to discover that they may not be of the right profile to use the scheme, it is still their decision.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What we want to do is to help him, at least, to understand whether he is suitable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to discourage financial intermediaries from proactively selling products to CPF members because investment churning could actually erode investment returns.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Third, we are going to review the types of asset classes offered under CPFIS to see if they are appropriate for growing retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to encourage members to invest for the long term and provide members with a diversified portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will announce these changes after we have finalised them later this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As recommended by the CPF Advisory Panel, LRIS will have low fees, simple investment choices, investments that are passively managed and mechanisms to encourage long-term investment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When we put together these schemes, CPF members will have three ways to grow their CPF savings in future: risk-free CPF interest rates, CPFIS and LRIS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to allow members the option of starting their CPF LIFE payout, with a lower initial payout which can then be escalating at 2% a year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those who are already on Standard and Basic Plans, they will have one year to switch into this new option if they want to.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: CPF Board will provide further details later this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon asked if we should make company medical plans portable for individuals with pre-existing illnesses who have left the company.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, MOM will have no intention to intervene in the market.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will leave it to the insurance market to decide.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Three ways to grow your savings: CPF risk-free interest, CPFIS and LRIS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When you turn 55, three options for the retirement sum: Basic, Full and Enhanced.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And when you reach the age of 65, three options for CPF LIFE payout: Basic, Standard and Escalating.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We revamped the Yearly Statement of Accounts last year and adopted a pictorial format.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We also provided customised tips for each member.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are glad that the members find the new format easier to understand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: CPF Board will also continue to reach out to members in the community through CPF retirement planning roadshows and mobile service centres as well as through mainstream and social media.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, CPF Board piloted a CPF Retirement Planning Service for members who are reaching 55, in other words, at the age of 54.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We invited 1,200 members to test out this service and 95% of them said they would recommend this service to their friends.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These one-on-one sessions help members to understand better the CPF schemes and the options available to them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We hope that members will make good use of the options available to better meet their retirement needs, as well as those of their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, OECD and several international studies commonly refer to workers in the economy as workers on the "Platform Economy".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These online platforms serve as intermediaries to match or connect service buyers with workers who take up short-term or piecemeal jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, there is matching of supply to demand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: From the economic angle, such online platforms create opportunities for businesses, workers and customers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They allow businesses to tap on workers who are available "on-demand" to serve customers more flexibly and responsively so as to reduce costs and increase revenues.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They also allow individuals to market their skills, provide their services to earn an income, and they can do so under a more flexible working arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: From the employment angle, my Ministry is monitoring closely their potential impact on the long-term well-being of the workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Common questions and concerns raised, including those raised by Mr Alex Yam, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Chen Show Mao and Ms Jessica Tan are: how different is gig work from traditional employment?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Are gig workers adequately protected under our labour laws?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Will they save enough for their housing, medical and retirement?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, if a private car driver joins a transport company with an employment contract and takes on jobs offered via app, he is in the gig economy but he is still an employee protected by labour laws because he is on an employment contract with the car rental company, even if he is on a short-term employment contract with the car rental company.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There is no difference from other workers who are employed under what we call "contract of service".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But if he provides a service in return for a fee, without entering into any employer-employee relationship with any party and, at the same time, he is not overly constrained by the conditions imposed by the platform owner or service buyer, then this is no different from any freelancer that we know today under what we call the "contract for service".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If you are a gig worker providing a service under a "contract for service", you are a gig freelancer, but under a "contract of service", then you are a gig employee.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the gig freelancers under "contracts for service", they are known as own-account workers in our labour force surveys and they are considered as self-employed persons by CPF and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In short, "gig workers" can be gig employees or gig freelancers depending on his work arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To understand better the freelancer landscape arising from the rise in the gig economy in Singapore, we supplemented our annual comprehensive labour force survey with a more detailed survey on freelancing last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I shall now share some interesting findings with this House.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These are workers who freelance as their main job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is within the range of 8% to 10% of employed residents in the past 10 years based on our previous surveys.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The secondary freelancers are those who freelance part-time alongside other jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They have a primary job and freelancing is their secondary job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These would include students, housewives or retirees who take on side jobs for additional income.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are in freelancing because they prefer to be freelancers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Sixty-seven percentage points of the 81% are primary freelancers and 14 percentage points are secondary freelancers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The main reasons for choosing to freelance: more freedom, earning extra income, spending more time with their family.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The remaining 19% freelanced, even though it was not their preferred choice.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Sixteen percent of them are in primary, 2% in secondary.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This group, that is, 16%, about 32,700 were doing primary freelancing but it is not their preferred choice.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the group that I am most concerned about.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under Adapt and Grow, we hope we will be able to reach out to as many of them as possible and help them move into full-time employment because freelancing is not their preferred choice.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Fourth, the top freelancing occupations are still the traditional occupations.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The top three are taxi drivers, real estate agents and working proprietors, such as provision shop owners and other business owners with no employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The other major freelancing occupations with more than 10,000 freelancers are insurance agents, private hire car drivers, hawker/stallholders and private tutors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Fifth, freelancers who use Internet platforms, also known as online intermediaries, to find work in the gig economy are still a minority.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The largest group is private hire car drivers: the Uber and Grab drivers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many of us may have the impression that there are actually many more gig freelancers out there than the number reported in this survey of 20,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I wish to point out that these 20,000 are those who freelance regularly, both part-time or full-time, but it does not capture those who freelance occasionally or once in a while.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Also, traditional freelancers who do not actively make use of online intermediaries to find work are not considered as gig workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though they may have an online presence to market themselves, they are still not considered as gig workers, for example, sport coaches and music instructors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our future annual surveys will enable us to track if the number is growing and in which occupations.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Their top concern is whether they can find sufficient customers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As freelancers, customers are very important to them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They also have concerns over the lack of income security, for example, arising from work injuries, when attending training or going for skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some of them are also concerned about timely and complete payment from their clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last but not least, they are also concerned about their savings for housing and retirement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is because the number of freelancers may grow in our future economy in tandem with the growth of the platform economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee has asked how MOM will gather views of relevant stakeholders and safeguard the interests of freelancers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Foo Mee Har has also offered her four suggestions in terms of how we can take care of the well-being of the freelancers better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about reviewing the Trade Union Act to allow freelancers to become NTUC union members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Trade Union Act, together with IRA and the Trade Disputes Act, regulate industrial relations between employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Hence, this set of legislation is not applicable to freelancers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But this does not mean that freelancers today cannot join NTUC as members for NTUC to champion their interests.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A good example is that many taxi drivers are freelancers with no employer and are today NTUC-U Associate members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we support NTUC in reaching out to more freelancers in more occupations, including the gig freelancers, and will be happy to work with NTUC and SNEF to pursue this issue further through the tripartite workgroup on freelancing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There is potential upside, there is potential downside, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, our challenge is to maximise the upside and minimise the downside.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I just have a couple of questions for the Minister on the newly-announced Attach-and-Train programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, if there are any training courses or programmes which the person on attachment is going through, or will be required to go through, will that training or course be fully paid or fully subsidised?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, the Minister mentioned earlier that the target group of this scheme are PMETs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: So, are we also opening it to all workers of all ages as well as including the rank-and-file workers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fourth, will the company then be obliged to hire these workers after the attachment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fifth, as we roll out this scheme, I hope employers as well as MOM will watch over these people on attachment because I am just concerned that they are not treated fairly and are being used as cheap labour.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is because of this timing gap between the hiring and the time needed for conversion.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said that, we are mindful of the potential downside of the Attach-and-Train programme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the reason why we have no intention to roll out Attach-and-Train across all the 50 PCPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I have earlier explained the selection criteria to minimise the danger that the trainees may eventually not be able to find jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Hence, we will only be working with sectors where there is a growing demand for such PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The PCP programme right now is open to PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Whether we need to have a PCP for rank-and-file, I am open to the idea.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I mentioned earlier in my speech, looking ahead to the future economy, we are going to see less distinction between PMETs and rank-and-file.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, we do need to upgrade the rank-and-file job as well, to professionalise them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in the case of logistics, we are working very closely with the Singapore Logistics Association.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They will be the ones helping us to screen the candidates, select the candidates.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They will be the ones to help us to find companies among their members to provide the attachment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, it is a safeguard to make sure that the programmes will not be abused.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I can assure the House that these partners that we have, they are all reliable partners, responsible partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When they make arrangements with their industry members, they also take on the responsibility to make sure that these companies taking them on attachment are, likewise, responsible employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I believe the Member is referring to a study by WEF where, on a global basis, they projected that, given the nature of work and the distribution between male and female, it is likely that more of the jobs performed by females can be displaced by technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said that, I will say that the employment profile between Singapore and the rest of the world is quite different in terms of education level, in terms of our deployment in STEM jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, we will still continue to encourage a more balanced form of engagement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But at the end of the day, I want to basically express that the impact of technology will be on everyone, whether male or female, young or old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But I took pain in my speech earlier to emphasise that fearing technology is not the way to go because, at the end of the day, all countries, all enterprises, will have no choice but to tap on technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Two companies, assuming they are identical in their business and so on, company A employs 100 workers – male, female, young and old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Company A, due to global competition, decides to embrace technology, so they use robots, IT and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, instead of 100 persons, they became more manpower-lean and now need only 90 persons.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But because they are more manpower-lean, they would be able, hopefully, to offer products cheaper, better, faster – the point mentioned by Mr Thomas Chua during the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When they are able to compete in a cheaper, better, faster way, their market share will grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, instead of $100 million, it may grow to $110 million, $120 million, and take away business from the company that did not respond.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, as the company continues to grow over time, even though they are manpower-lean, in fact, their workforce can actually grow, except that the growth in their workforce will be slower than the growth in their business revenue.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, it is very important that, in Singapore, we do not look at technology as our competitor for jobs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Lastly, I would like to know how these potential leaders are identified and groomed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But let me also explain upfront that LDI is today a programme driven by MTI.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But having said so, MOM, in fact, is a strong supporter of LDI.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The reason why I said so is because we believe that the development of a strong Singaporean Core should not be measured just in terms of numbers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is not about whether in any sector, in any company, what percentage are Singaporeans and what percentage are not.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is just a quantitative measurement of the strength of the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What is more important is to look at whether we can strengthen the Singaporean Core at all levels, from the entry level all the way to the top.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is the reason why SkillsFuture, led by SSG – in fact, tomorrow, Members can ask Minister Ong Ye Kung to explain even better – under SkillsFuture, we make sure that we have support programmes all the way from internship to Earn and Learn and all the way to the leadership development initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: MOM will go all out to support EDB and MTI in the development of LDI.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, I mentioned that we have formed a committee in what we call the Human Capital Partners (HCPs).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The HCPs are our employers who believe in nurturing human capital.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, one of the core priorities of HCP is to nurture what we call the "Glocal talents".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These are local talents who are good enough to perform regional and global roles. "Local", you add the "g" in front, it becomes "glocal".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, "glocal talents" are our local talents who are good enough and are as good as global talent.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under HCP, the nurturing of glocal talent will be one of the key thrusts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if a company feels that it has enough commitment in doing so, they can step forward and say, "Look, I want to join the HCP community." Now, who will identify the person to be nurtured into the glocal talent?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is not for us to go into the company and say, "Look, you should nurture this person or that person".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, I have shared the example of the applied material case where Ms Yvonne was identified by her company and has proven that she is good enough for the job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: She was able to live up to the expectation and, as a result, today, she is a senior manufacturing director, and the product line that she is responsible for, in fact, is one of their so-called product lead throughout applied material globally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: First, I think workplace accidents are often the result of poor coordination in workplaces, especially in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The second question I have is whether MOM can do more to encourage near-miss reporting at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I believe the Minister of State missed this point earlier.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We would require them to hold meetings at the worksite to pass down the message, communicate with one another so that there will be proper supervision and coordination to reduce worksite accidents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I am sorry that I did not address this point just now because of time constraints.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, now, I would like to take the opportunity to allay his concern.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM and also the WSH Council have been actively advocating the reporting and also the monitoring of near misses at worksites.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: If we are able to encourage this as part of the WSH system in every company, every near miss incident reported can prevent the next accident from happening.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is something that we are working very closely on with the WSH Council.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Just last week, I received some photographs on this platform by a former Member of Parliament who observed some unsafe worksite practices.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: He sent the pictures to me and, immediately, I got somebody to go to the worksite.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The beauty of this upgraded Snap@MOM is that it will not be linked to MOM.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: All near miss incidents reported will be confined within the company, so that MOM will not go down to investigate.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: But it is for the company, the management, to take responsibility to investigate to make sure that they do something to right the wrong.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, I hope I have addressed the Member's queries.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The consideration is upon investigating on their valid claims or non-payment of salaries.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: While we are investigating and trying to find out about the facts of the claim, we do not want the workers to be unproductive.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, there is an arrangement for them, if they so request, to transfer employers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: That can be facilitated by MWC to enable them to continue to be productive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I think one of the things that the Minister mentioned made a lot of sense, that is, low cost.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: But I would like to ask the Minister to clarify that when he mentioned "passive", I think it has raised concerns among people in the industry because no retirement scheme, if it is an investment, can be passive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: At the least, it needs to be able to meet the needs of members at different life stages.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, for younger people, you can take a little bit more risk; nearer to your retirement, you have to make sure you preserve.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Of course, the system can do that, but it cannot be passive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: If I can ask the Minister to make sure that that is accounted for.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is the reason why we have to design LRIS such that he or she would be putting his/her money under LRIS passively, as a passive investment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But somebody has to work for his/her money.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There would be fund managers to manage the fund for him/her.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The member himself or herself does not have to make active decisions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Can I clarify with the Minister whether this scheme is open to any rank-and-file worker looking to switch industries or must he be unemployed for a certain period of time first?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Is it across all industries or only specific industries?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The longer they are unemployed, the harder it is for us to bring them back to work.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is the reason why last year, we started this scheme called work trial just to test out the concept.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As it turned out, the feedback has been very positive because we have the confidence of jobseekers as well as the confidence of employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the reason we have decided to expand the programme to make it more attractive and, at the same time, make it longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Member asked whether we would expand this programme to the non-LTU workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say that our main purpose is to help workers to get jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If the worker is prepared to try out the work, why not?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The question of whether this is available to all sectors, it is available to all sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our challenge is more to find employers who are prepared to join the scheme.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Basically, I would like to ask the Minister whether he would consider a work trial for our PMETs who want to look at other industries before they switch over permanently.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: So, it would be worthwhile looking at it.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: The second question I have is with regard to PCP.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: For some of the programmes, the training is beyond 18 months.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: For instance, nursing is 24 months for someone who is not in the industry at all.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Can the wage support or some form of support be given to these people and the industries that are taking them?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This will help, especially the Intermediate and Long-Term Care sector, which is taking in nurses who want to switch over from one industry to another?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: I remember MOM stating that there will be a HR framework and to make sure that the HR professionals are up to skill and professionalism.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, maybe you can work with the NTUC, the Labour Movement to see whether we can try this, probably under the future job, future skill programme led by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the second point about the PCP longer than 18 months, we support PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, is the question whether it can be extended beyond 18 months?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: For some sectors like nursing, it takes 24 months to train a person.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: It would be worthwhile to consider extending this wage support beyond that.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will provide a certain level of wage support, training support, but our partners, it could be MOH or other agencies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: IMDA, for example, what they do is that they take our basic PCP, they add something on top called "PCP plus" and "PCP plus, plus".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the Member's suggestion, I think we can take it up with MOH.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last, but not least, on the HR professionals, I thank the Member for bringing up this point.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The reason why I did not touch on this is because, like what Mr Sam Tan said, we ran out of time and no Member raised this issue.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, I can assure the Member that we are making some major move to upgrade the HR community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will include the so-called professional certification of the HR community.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Members should expect to hear our announcement by the middle of this year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A lot of the points that the Minister has raised seem to be more pro-workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While I understand why something has to be done, I think businesses and employers are also the ones who create jobs to keep the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Can the Minister explain how he would intend to strike a better balance in future in some of the schemes?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I must apologise if I have come across as simply pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In my conclusion, I did highlight that whatever we do, we have to be pro-worker and pro-business, both at the same time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If one is weak, the other one cannot be strong.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With that in mind, if I can revisit the four keys that I talked about for this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The first one is about transform and grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Transform and grow is both pro-worker and pro-business because, as we heard from Minister of State Teo Ser Luck, all the 2,000 companies under LEDS, whatever they have done − automation, mechanisation and so on − is good for their business and, at the same time, good for the workers because by being more manpower-lean, as a result, the workers are more productive, their wages have improved and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, transform and grow is both pro-worker and pro-business.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Again, Adapt and Grow we believe is both pro-worker and pro-business.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The third aspect is about building an inclusive workforce, at the same time strengthening the complementarity between local and foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Again, we believe that the mindset of "2/3 plus 1/3" is greater than one that is not only pro-workers but pro-businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many of our companies under HCP are all doing very well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The reason why they are doing well is because they value manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They look at their staff not as human resource but as human capital.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I asked one of them what is the difference between human resource and human capital.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They said resource normally is for consumption and it will depreciate over time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But capital is what you invest in and it will appreciate over time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, our third thrust is both pro-workers and pro-businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe this is both pro-workers and pro-businesses as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In closing, I thank my fellow Parliamentary colleagues who filed their cuts and shared their thoughts, views and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I believe we have thrown greater light on the challenges we face as a country and the right things we must do to transform and grow and adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I also want to thank the Permanent Secretary, Deputy Secretaries and the MOM team, Workforce Singapore, CPF Board as well as SLF for their hard work behind the scenes.
